blocks.x: This card is a one-page reference. It holds four instructions that apply throughout the workbook.
Where this comes from

This workbook was not written about your circumstances specifically. It draws on decades of SafeCare’s clinical work with men who have sexually offended against children. Not every page will match your situation. Work on the ones that do. What applies to you now may be different in a year, so read everything again at each review.
Who to talk to

Where a page says to talk to someone, please speak with a trusted professional such as your psychologist. When you are unsure about something, be especially cautious. It is important that you discuss the feelings that come up with someone qualified. If you cannot reach one, see your GP or call the mental health line for your state or territory.
What you will write here
This workbook is yours. Keep it somewhere private.

Write in detail. Write what was happening at the time, where you were, what you were thinking and feeling, what you told yourself, and what you did in the lead-up. Write dates, places and the names of people in your support network, so that each answer is something you can act on later.
The intention is to remind yourself of the decisions you made, so that you can learn from them and make better decisions in the future.

For your protection, do not describe your offending behaviour or the child. Under Australian law, a written description of a child in a sexual context can be illegal material, even in a private workbook.
How the example pages work

Most worksheets end with an example page. It shows one ordinary answer so that you can see how much detail to include. Do not copy this example; write your own. It then shows a few weak answers with their faults marked. First drafts tend to go wrong in the same few ways, and the example page shows you some of them.
What this set is

This is one document out of five that belong together. You may have been given all five at once, or one at a time as you reach each stage of a programme, or some of them years apart with nobody giving them to you at all. However you came to this one, read all of it before any of the other four, because it explains what the other four can and cannot do for you.
The five, in the order they are meant to be read.
This preamble.
Understanding My Past, seventeen short concepts plus two further ones on risk and protective factors, drawn from the SafeCare programme.
Planning My Future, a workbook for building the life you want, once you have a clearer idea of how you got here.
A Relapse Prevention Plan, for staying on track once a plan exists.
A Clinician’s Framework, written for a treating professional, though nothing in it is off limits to you.
Where two of these cover the same ground, treat the earlier one in this list as the foundation. The later one builds on it and refers back to it by name instead of repeating it.
Why write this down
Before you start, a fair question: does doing this make any difference, or is it paperwork?

It has been looked at. Two studies in New Zealand followed men released after sexual offences against children. Before release, each man had a plan for his life on the outside. It covered where he was going to live, what work he was going to do, who was going to be around him and what support he had arranged. Researchers rated how good those plans were, then waited to see what happened.
The men with better plans went on to offend less, and the men with poor plans offended more.

The finding is about how good the plan was, and having a plan was not enough. A plan that was vague, or borrowed from somebody else, or written to satisfy whoever was asking for it, went with a worse outcome than a plan that was detailed and honest.
What you write in these books is not a formality and it is not for your file. The care you put into it is what makes it work.
What this set cannot do
This material has limits, and they are listed here.

This set of five documents has not been independently evaluated as a whole. Individual ideas in it draw on tested research, cited where they come up, but the combination and the wording are this project’s own.

Some of what you will read, particularly the parts describing a person as having three parts, comes from clinical practice and not from published, peer-reviewed research. Where that is the case, the text says so at that point.
None of this replaces a psychologist. This set does not assume that somebody is looking over your shoulder.
What to watch for

Copying a worked example instead of writing your own. Every example in this set is deliberately the most obvious, ordinary answer there is, so that copying it does not help you. A plan assembled from examples looks complete and is worthless, and if you are working alone, you are the only one who can tell the difference.
Treating a low number anywhere in this set, such as a rating, a score or a slipped need, as a verdict on you. A low number is information, and it tells you something early enough to act on.

Using any part of this material to work out how close you can get to a line, instead of how to stay well clear of it. If you notice yourself doing that, stop and raise it with your psychologist. Noticing it is the result you want: it means the warning sign is working.
About the harm

blocks.head: Before you start
blocks.x: What happened caused harm to a real child. If part of what happened involved an image or a recording, that image or recording is not separate from the harm. It is a record of something that happened to that child, and every time that record is used, that child is used again. Distance, whether in time, in place, or through a screen, does not make the harm smaller. It only makes the harm harder to see from where you are standing.
Before you go further

Everything in the four documents that follow this one assumes you accept that what happened caused real harm to a real person. This document cannot check that you do, and you can turn the page whatever you decide right now.
The set asks this of you anyway, because everything after it depends on that acceptance being honest. Without it, what you write in the boxes that follow cannot do its work.
Measuring your progress

The urges, thoughts or feelings connected to what happened may get easier to manage over time, or they may not. If they do not, that does not mean you are failing, and it does not mean something is wrong with you that is not wrong with anybody else in this position.

Measure how quickly you notice the feeling when it turns up, and how quickly you recover once you have noticed it, rather than whether the feeling ever fully goes away. Those two times can keep improving in a year when the underlying feeling does not change at all, so track them instead.
Where to start

Understanding My Past comes next in the reading order, and is the better starting point if you have a copy of it. Planning a life in Planning My Future is hard when you have not yet worked out what went wrong in the one you had. If you have only been given Planning My Future, it is written to stand on its own and does not assume you have read the other one first.
Nothing in this document, or anywhere else in this concept series, explains away anything you did. Everything else here depends on you accepting that before you go on.
Where the line sits

The SafeCare book puts the distinction plainly: explanations are not excuses, and nothing excuses this. But the book also asks a second question straight after the first: without explanations, how does anyone, the person who offended included, ever get anywhere with stopping it happening again? Refusing to look at where something came from does not make you more accountable; it means you go on not understanding the thing you most need to understand about yourself.
What this looks like

Take an ordinary example unrelated to offending: a man who grew up in a house where the only way to be heard was to shout learns to shout. Explaining that tells you where the habit came from and what it was doing for him at the time, but it does not tell you that the people around him now deserve to be shouted at. The explanation and the excuse are two different sentences, even though they start from the same fact.

The concepts in this series work the same way. Each one explains something about how you got here. None of them, on its own or added together, decides whether you were responsible for what you did. That question was already answered before you opened this document, and nothing in here reopens it.
Why this concept matters

Christabel Chamarette’s own clinical experience, drawn from decades of treating people who had sexually offended, was that understanding where the impulse to offend came from helped the person take responsibility for it, not avoid it. Becoming more conscious of an impulse is what makes it possible to catch and manage. Staying in the dark about it does not protect anyone, it just leaves the same pattern free to run again unnoticed.
Responsibility for the offending lies with the person who offended. That does not change no matter what this concept series explains about how they got there.

What she found in practice runs against a common assumption. Men rarely use their own childhood or history as an excuse themselves. Using somebody’s history to argue for a lighter outcome is usually done by a lawyer in a courtroom, not by a man doing the work of understanding himself. You may be holding back from this series because you worry that looking at where things came from will make you a man who makes excuses. Her experience across a great many cases says the opposite is closer to true.

blocks.head: The excuse trap
blocks.x: People sometimes finish a concept in this series and use what they read as a reason the offending was not their fault. None of these documents say that. An explanation can be completely accurate and the same person is still responsible. If you notice yourself building an argument for why you were not to blame, stop and call it an excuse. Noticing that in yourself is the skill this document teaches.

units.title: Understanding and Responsibility

blocks.x: Four boxes. The first is practice on other people’s sentences. The last three are about you.
1. Explanations and excuses
Finish each sentence with either “an explanation” or “an excuse.” An explanation says why something happened. An excuse says why it should not count.
a.	His car broke down on the way, so he arrived forty minutes late. This is  explanation  excuse.
b.	He said the meeting probably was not that important anyway, so it did not matter that he missed it. This is  explanation  excuse.
c.	She grew up in a house where nobody ever explained anything, so she never learned how to ask for help. This is  explanation  excuse.
d.	She said anybody raised the way she was would have ended up the same, so there was nothing to be done about it. This is  explanation  excuse.
e.	He had not slept properly in days and snapped at his brother over something small. This is  explanation  excuse.
f.	He said his brother should have known better than to bring it up when he was tired. This is  explanation  excuse.

Answers: explanation, excuse, explanation, excuse, explanation, excuse. Every pair describes the same kind of situation. The first sentence in each pair only says why. The second argues that the outcome should not count, or that no other outcome was possible. That argument is the excuse.
2. Two of your own
Write one ordinary explanation from your own life, something true about why you did something, that does not argue the thing did not matter.
Now write one ordinary excuse from your own life, something you have said or thought that argued an outcome should not count.
3. What explains your own path
Write about what was going on for you and what you were feeling or trying to get from it. Do not describe the offending.
In the same form as section 1’s explanation sentences, what is one true thing that explains something about how you got here?
4. Limits of the explanation
Now that you have written that explanation, what has it not decided, and who already decided it?

checks: Your section 2 excuse argues an outcome should not count, it does not just restate a fact.
Your section 3 answer explains, it does not argue you were not responsible.
Your section 4 answer says outright who is responsible, not just “it does not decide everything.”
Nothing you have written describes how the offending was carried out, only what was going on for you.

examples.x: A good answer

examples.label: Good answer to box 2
examples.x: Explanation: I missed my sister’s birthday call because I was scared she would ask about the case, and it felt easier to just not pick up. Excuse: I told myself she probably would not have noticed either way.
examples.why: The pair is ordinary, and that is why it works. The explanation gives a feeling, being scared, and a choice, not picking up, and it does not argue that the missed call did not matter. The excuse does argue that: it exists to make the missed call not count. Both sentences describe the same evening, but only the excuse tries to get him off the hook for it.

examples.x: Common pitfalls

examples.label: Weak answer to box 1
examples.x: He marked every calm-sounding sentence as an explanation and every frustrated-sounding one as an excuse, without checking whether it actually argued the outcome should not count.
examples.why: The test is whether the sentence argues the thing should not count, since a calm sentence can still be an excuse and an upset one can still be an honest explanation. Sorting by mood gets the easy pairs right by accident and the harder ones from real life wrong.

examples.label: Weak answer to box 3
examples.x: The answer gives an honest feeling from around that time, then adds that, given everything going on, it is hard to see how things could have gone any other way.
examples.why: The first half is what this box asks for. The second half is the kind of excuse sentence from section 1, disguised as an explanation: it argues that no other outcome was possible instead of saying what was going on. If your own answer starts arguing that the outcome could not have gone another way, that is the trap this concept describes. It can feel like a deeper level of honesty, but it is an excuse.

examples.label: Weak answer to box 4
examples.x: It does not decide everything. Nobody’s life is simple.
examples.why: This never says what the explanation does not decide, which is responsibility for the offending, or who decided it, which is the person who offended. A true-sounding generality takes the place of the one sentence this box asks for.

examples.x: The first is an easy mistake in a comprehension exercise. The second is the trap this concept describes, turning up where it is most likely to. The third is too general to decide anything. Review your own answers above against these three.

blocks.x: SafeCare ran this work in groups, and groups helped, but the group was never the mechanism. What did the work was saying a true thing out loud to another person who could hear it and respond. A room of other men was one way to get that. A psychologist, or one person you trust, can do the same job. This concept is about that mechanism.
What another person adds

SafeCare found, across the people it worked with, that keeping something secret puts a barrier between a person and everyone around them, and that this isolation is uncomfortable and is also a risk in itself. It also found the opposite: hearing somebody else describe their own childhood out loud sometimes brought back a memory of your own that private reflection had never reached. Hearing another person’s account, instead of only imagining it, reached memories that thinking alone did not.
Why this concept matters

This document asks you to write a great deal, in private, in worksheets nobody else has to see. Writing helps, but a page cannot hear you, cannot respond, cannot notice when something does not add up, and cannot remember what you said last time and check it against what you are saying now. See What People Tell Themselves, which describes building an outside voice into your own thinking. This concept is the earlier, more basic version of that. Sometimes the outside voice has to belong to somebody else, because your own head has blind spots that private reflection does not reach.

blocks.head: The excuse trap
blocks.x: One trap is treating a page you have written as equivalent to a thing you have said to a person, because writing it down felt hard enough. The two are not equivalent. Another is deciding that because something was said once, to one person, a while ago, it never needs saying again. Disclosure is not a single past event, and it has to keep happening as your life changes.

blocks.x: SafeCare’s Intro module used a well-known academic framework, Finkelhor’s model, which sets out four separate barriers that would all need to fail for offending to happen. This concept turns that around. Instead of analysing how each barrier failed, it asks you to check whether each one is standing now and will keep standing for the rest of your life.
The three you can build

blocks.head: Why only three
blocks.x: Finkelhor’s model has four barriers. The fourth concerns a specific child’s own resistance. It is not included here, in any form, because describing it would mean providing the kind of material this document set never provides, in any framing. This concept does not need it: its job is to check the three you are responsible for keeping standing.
Barrier one: it holds

Your own values and self-control are the first barrier, and having them is not the same as them holding under pressure. Both What People Tell Themselves and Saying It Out Loud are about checking this barrier against an outside voice. The alternative is trusting it alone, in your own head.
Barrier two: people who notice
The Circle of Safety is this barrier, built deliberately: people who are briefed and actively involved, and who would notice and respond.
Barrier three: no opportunity
The same Circle of Safety is also this barrier, from a different angle: not managing opportunity moment to moment through willpower, but removing it structurally, so the opportunity does not arise.
Why this concept matters
Relying on only the first one, “I would never,” is the pattern that failed before. All three, standing together, do a job that none of them can do alone.

blocks.head: The excuse trap
blocks.x: Believing barrier one is enough on its own, because it is the one that feels most like character and least like admitting you need anything external, is an easy way to misuse this framework. A person who says “I don’t need a circle, I would just never do it again” is describing the barrier that failed before, standing on its own.

blocks.x: Planning My Future, the workbook later in this series, is built on one idea: every need is ordinary, and the route taken to meet it is what counts. A boundary keeps that route fair to the other person. This concept builds the general skill of spotting when a boundary has been crossed without anyone remarking on it, using ordinary examples first and then your own life.
Reading a boundary

When a boundary is respected, the need still gets met, with the other person’s informed agreement, appropriate to the relationship. A crossed boundary does not always look dramatic. It often looks like one person’s need being met steadily at the other person’s cost, while the person benefiting describes it as normal or says the other person does not mind.
Why this concept matters

SafeCare found that recognising this pattern first in ordinary situations, ones unrelated to offending, made it far easier to recognise in the specific relationship that mattered most. Later in this series, Adult Closeness asks a version of the same question about where your closeness comes from now. This concept builds the lens.

blocks.head: The excuse trap
blocks.x: The trap is deciding that because the other person seemed willing, or did not object, or even seemed to enjoy it, the boundary must have been fine. Willingness differs from an honest, informed, equal choice, especially where one person has more power, more age, or more authority than the other. Reading calm or compliance as consent is the mistake this concept exists to catch.

blocks.x: Picture a jar with thick sides and a tight lid. Everybody is born with one, and everybody’s jar starts out empty.
What the jar holds

As childhood unfolds, the jar begins to fill with feelings that had nowhere to go at the time, not only anger, but grief, sadness and loss as well. When it is full, the contents press on the sides, which is your body, and on the lid, which is the gateway between you and the outside world. Pressure on the sides can show up as headaches, stomach aches, or being unwell in ways that never quite explain themselves, and pressure on the lid is what makes the feelings hard to keep down.

Some jars fill young, if childhood held violence or abuse. Some take decades. Either way, a full jar looks for somewhere to go, and it finds it one of three ways. One is a short-term release that eases the pressure for a while and always needs more of itself to keep working. Another is a stronger lid built from sheer will or constant busyness. The third is the lid coming off entirely, all at once, often triggered by something far smaller than the pressure behind it. Everyday versions of that last one are what people call road rage or supermarket rage. The reaction is wildly out of proportion to whatever set it off, because the person on the receiving end is rarely what it is about.
Why this concept matters

A jar that has been filling since childhood, with nowhere safe to put what is in it, is under a lot of pressure by adulthood. Pressure with nowhere sanctioned to go finds a way out, whether or not that way is a good one. Knowing what is in your own jar is one of the more direct ways of lowering the pressure that a harmful route was, at some point, being used to relieve. So is building lasting release valves for it instead of the short-term ones that need more each time.

blocks.head: The excuse trap
blocks.x: People sometimes finish this section and say their offending was the jar overflowing. This section does not say that. A full jar explains why you were carrying pressure. It does not explain why the pressure came out where it did, and it does not decide who is responsible. A person can carry a full jar their whole life and never harm anybody. The jar accounts for the pressure, not for the choice.

units.title: Pseudo Adult, Inner Child, True Adult

blocks.x: This concept introduces three parts of a person that the SafeCare model uses throughout the rest of this series and that Planning My Future, the workbook that comes after this one, assumes you know. If anything past this point mentions your Inner Child or your True Adult without explaining them again, this is the concept to return to.
Which part is speaking

The Pseudo Adult is the grown-up front you learned to put on, the face the world sees. The Inner Child is the part of you that got stuck at the age when something happened that you could not handle at the time. Neither one is a flaw. Everybody has both.
The True Adult is the grown-up child, made up of all three parts, and its job is to act as the umpire between the other two.

An umpire needs two sides on the field. The Inner Child does not go anywhere and is not meant to: it is not a stage you get past or something to be got rid of. The True Adult listens to the front, listens to the child, and decides. It does not silence either of them, and it never stops having the job.
What this looks like

A man who grew up needing to seem fine all the time builds a strong Pseudo Adult, the calm, competent front that gets him through the day. Underneath it, the Inner Child still has whatever that childhood left unresolved. When something touches that old feeling, in an argument, under stress, at the smallest criticism, the Inner Child’s reaction can come out through the Pseudo Adult’s grown-up voice. That can be confusing to everyone in the room, including him. The True Adult’s job is to notice that this is what is happening and decide what needs to happen next. It does not let the Pseudo Adult pretend nothing is going on, and it does not let the Inner Child drive.
Why this concept matters

When the Inner Child’s needs go unrecognised, they do not disappear. They come out sideways, in ways an adult would not choose if he were deciding. Planning My Future gives the same account, that offending was an ordinary need met through a harmful route, seen from a different angle. The eleven needs that workbook works through belong to that same Inner Child, and meeting them properly, as an adult, out in the open, is how the True Adult does its job.

blocks.head: The excuse trap
blocks.x: People sometimes finish this section believing the goal is to grow out of the Inner Child altogether, to become one single, fully integrated adult with no separate parts left. This model does not say that, and believing you have already got there is a risk in itself, because that is the moment the umpire stops watching the field. The Inner Child does not go anywhere. The job is to keep the True Adult listening permanently.

blocks.x: SafeCare found, across decades of practice, that offending often runs in families and does not usually appear once, out of nowhere. Seeing that pattern in your own family does not excuse anything and does not accuse anyone, and it gives you information you can act on.
Reading the pattern back

The tool for seeing it is a genogram, a simple family diagram. Circles mark the women in a family, squares mark the men. Two more marks matter here: an x for a family member known to have offended, and a v for a family member known to have been a victim. SafeCare routinely found that the person in front of them was not the first x to appear in their own family’s map.

One pattern showed up often enough to check against your own history. Comparing the age of a person’s victim with what was going on in his own life at that age sometimes turned up a connection. The connection was something unresolved that had happened to him at almost the same age as the person he later offended against. It does not happen in every case, and every family is different, so look for it instead of assuming it is absent.
Why this concept matters

A pattern you cannot see is a pattern you cannot manage. If your map shows a connection between your history and your offending, treat it as a vulnerability to watch from now on. It is not a verdict on you, and it is not something to keep to yourself. It matters to anyone else in your family who may share the pattern and has no way to see it yet.

blocks.head: The excuse trap
blocks.x: Some people look at a family map full of x’s and conclude the outcome was fixed from the start, an excuse that looks like an explanation. A pattern in a family raises the chance of it appearing again but does not guarantee it, and an x on your family map does not make you one. What runs in a family is a raised chance. It explains a vulnerability. It does not decide what you do.

blocks.head: Keep this page private
blocks.x: A completed four-generation family map can be subpoenaed if it exists on paper or on a shared device. Use it to see a pattern, and do not leave it where other people can find it as a family record. Keep the worksheet somewhere only you control, on a device or in a place nobody else can access. If you have a lawyer, ask them what to do with it once you have used it.

blocks.x: This concept gives you a way to think back over your own childhood without dismissing something serious and without feeling shame over something that was ordinary. Use it for looking back at your own history, not at any child now.
The continuum

Professionals who work in this area describe a continuum, not a single line: normal, inappropriate, problematic, abusive, violent. Ordinary curiosity between children of a similar age, with no secrecy demanded and neither child holding power over the other, is at the normal end. Behaviour involving a clear age or power gap, coercion, or an adult is well past it. Ordinary curiosity is part of growing up, and adults, including parents, are rarely taught how to tell it from something that is not. That leads to a common mistake.

A parent who reacts to a child’s ordinary curiosity with alarm can teach the child that bodies and sex are shameful or frightening instead of private. A calm, matter-of-fact response to something ordinary causes far less harm than an alarmed one. If you have felt shame since childhood over something that was ordinary, you did nothing to earn that shame.
Why this concept matters

Sorting your own memories against this continuum does two things. It can lift shame from things that were never past the ordinary end, so you stop spending energy on it, and it can also show where something in your own history did cross a line. Either finding gives you a better starting point for Your Family Map and Patterns: age, gender and form than denying it happened or assuming everything did.

blocks.head: The excuse trap
blocks.x: Some people use this continuum to decide that everything in their own childhood, or in what they later did themselves, was probably normal, since children explore. The continuum is for telling the difference between the two. If you are unsure where something sits, raise it with your psychologist, and take the more cautious reading instead of deciding it yourself in whichever direction feels most comfortable.

blocks.x: This concept asks you to state three plain facts about who you offended against: age, gender, and the kind of relationship it was. It does not ask you to explain why you did it. Later in this series, Warning Signs and the Safety Plan Card and The Circle of Safety ask you to plan around situations from your own life. A plan cannot be built around a pattern you have not stated plainly first.
Stating the facts
Age

Your Family Map already asked you to compare the age of the person you offended against with what was happening, unresolved, in your own life at around that same age. This concept does not ask that question again. It asks you to bring the answer forward, because it belongs alongside the other two facts below.
Gender

State the gender of the person or people you offended against, plainly, as a fact, without explaining it. Linking a victim’s gender to your own history of being abused, or to your own sexuality, has never been shown to predict anything reliably, and it usually works as an excuse. State the fact. Leave the theory alone.
Form

Say what kind of relationship it was: your own child or step-child, another family member, the child of a partner or a friend. Or it may have been a child you had in your care through work, coaching, or another position of trust, or a child you did not know beforehand. Only the category of relationship is needed here, not how anything happened, because a safety plan has to be built around the relationship.
Why this concept matters

A pattern you have not stated plainly is a pattern you cannot plan around. Knowing that your own pattern involves, for example, a particular age range, someone in your own family, or a position of trust is not a prediction and not a life sentence. That knowledge is the specific information that turns the next few concepts in this series from a general list into a plan for your own life.

blocks.head: The excuse trap
blocks.x: Two habits get in the way here. The first is using a theory, usually about gender, to explain the pattern away instead of stating it. The second is deciding that because it happened once, or with one person, there is no pattern to plan around. Both stop this page doing its job. A pattern of one is still a pattern to plan around, and explaining a fact does not make it safer.

blocks.head: Keep this page private
blocks.x: A page that records the age, gender and relationship pattern of who you offended against can be subpoenaed if it exists on paper or on a shared device. Use it to see a pattern and plan around it, and do not leave it where other people can find it as a record. Keep the worksheet somewhere only you control. If you have a lawyer, ask them what to do with it once you have used it.

blocks.x: SafeCare found that trying to build empathy for a victim before a person had any empathy for his own child self tended to produce performance, saying what treatment wants to hear, and no change in the person. This concept comes first for that reason. It stays inside your own history and does not ask you to write anything from a victim’s point of view.
The child you were
Pseudo Adult, Inner Child, True Adult described the part of you that got stuck at a particular age. This concept asks you to address that part of you in writing.
Why no guided exercise

Some programmes use a guided, spoken exercise to help a person access this material, a psychologist talking them through it slowly, in person. A printed page cannot do this safely, so it is not attempted here. If a guided version like that would help you, ask your psychologist directly, and leave the exercise out rather than looking for a written substitute.
What the worksheet asks

A short letter to your own child self, at the age Your Family Map or Patterns: age, gender and form already helped you locate, and a short reply written as that child self. SafeCare has run this exercise for years. You may find the letter easy and the reply harder, because comforting is a skill you may never have been shown.
Why this concept matters

A person who cannot recognise or meet his own child self’s needs tends to meet them indirectly, at somebody else’s expense, which is the mechanism Pseudo Adult, Inner Child, True Adult describes. Comforting that part of yourself, instead of silencing it or feeding it in secret, is the same skill the later work in this series uses. You practise it here on the safest subject, your own past.

blocks.head: The excuse trap
blocks.x: Two habits get in the way here. The first is turning the letter into another round of self-punishment: harsh, contemptuous, telling the child self what he deserved. SafeCare has seen this happen and has always had to correct it, because it defeats the purpose and teaches nothing new. The second is using “I was a hurt kid too” as a reason the offending makes sense. This concept does not minimise what you did. The skill it practises, comforting a part of yourself, has nothing to do with excusing it.

blocks.x: This concept asks you to draft an apology that is not sent, not shown to anyone, and not something you arrange to deliver. If a supported opportunity for something like this is ever offered, it would come through a witnessed professional process, not something you set up yourself, and this page is not for that. This page tests one thing: whether you know what a good apology looks like, because a first draft is easy to get wrong.
What an apology is for

SafeCare’s filmed apology exercise was reviewed many times, and the finding was the same each time: a good apology gives the child what the child needs. A bad apology gives the offender what the offender needs, usually forgiveness, reassurance, or an end to feeling terrible. The programme documented this example: “I feel so terrible that you can’t talk to me anymore. I miss you.” That sentence is about the writer, not the child, however sincerely it is meant.

More often than not, what a child needed was to be told plainly that the abuse was not their fault. They did not need an explanation of why it happened. Why it happened is a question for an adult to ask. An apology also asks for nothing back. “One day I hope you’ll be able to forgive me” asks the child for something, however gently.
What a good apology does
Takes full responsibility, plainly, without softening it.
Says clearly that it was not the child’s fault.
Does not explain why it happened.
Does not describe what happened.
Does not ask for anything back: not forgiveness, not contact, not reassurance, not sympathy.
Why this concept matters
The first instinct, drafting something like this, is often to write for your own relief. Testing a draft against these five things is a skill to have ready, whether or not you ever use it.

blocks.head: The excuse trap
blocks.x: SafeCare saw two failures most often. Each looks like an apology but does something else. One states how much the writer has suffered, hoping the child will feel sorry for him in return. The other hopes aloud for forgiveness, which is a request however softly made. Both put the offender’s feelings at the centre of a page that is supposed to be about the child’s. If your draft does either, it has failed in the way this exercise most often fails.

Write the apology you would want to give, before testing it against anything.

examples.x: A good answer

examples.label: Good answer to box 2
examples.x: It fails on “does not ask for anything back.” The last line says “I hope one day you’ll understand why,” which is still asking her to do something for me.

examples.x: Common pitfalls

examples.label: Weak answer to box 1
examples.x: I am so sorry for everything. I think about it every day and it has destroyed my life too. I hope you can understand that I was going through a lot back then. I just want you to know how much I regret it and that I am not a bad person.

It never says the sentence a child needed most: that it was not their fault. A first attempt often looks like this, which is why this exercise exists.

examples.label: Weak answer to box 3
examples.x: Changed “I hope you can understand that I was going through a lot back then” to “I hope you can understand that I was going through a lot back then, but I know that’s not an excuse.”

These are general findings from 35 people who were not connected to your own case, and they do not describe what anyone in your own life wants or needs. This concept is not a plan for contacting anyone, and it does not promise that doing these things earns forgiveness, contact, or anything else back.
What the research found
A researcher who had run SafeCare groups interviewed 35 adult survivors of intrafamilial child sexual abuse about what would have made their recovery easier. Several themes came up again and again.
What came up most often
An acknowledgement that the abuse happened, and that it was entirely the adult’s fault, not the child’s, even if the child seemed to go along with it or respond to the contact.
Knowing that looking fine afterward, doing well, staying close to the offender, appearing successful, never meant it had not mattered or had been forgiven.
Not being blamed for staying quiet. Silence was usually a survival strategy, weighing up what speaking up would cost the rest of the family, not agreement or enjoyment.
A non-judgemental professional service, for the family as a whole, rather than everyone being left to manage the aftermath alone.
Confidence that the offender would change, so nobody else was harmed the same way.

Some, not all, also wanted to be able to ask the offending parent why, later, in their own time. Several who wanted it also felt they had to hide it, from fear of hurting others or being misunderstood. This concept cannot tell you whether or when anyone in your own life wants any of this, and you do not get to decide or arrange it.
Why this concept matters

Some of what is on this list is yours to give, whether or not it is ever received. Some of it is appropriate only on the other person’s terms and timing, never yours, and some of it was never yours to give at all. You need to tell these apart, because offering what was never yours to offer, or withholding what was, causes harm in both directions.

blocks.head: The excuse trap
blocks.x: The trap here is treating this list as a checklist for earning something back: do enough of these and eventually there will be contact, or forgiveness, or relief. That turns a survivor’s stated needs into a transaction, which A Good Apology already described as the most common way an apology fails. The opposite trap is deciding that because you cannot know what any specific person wants, there is nothing you can do. Responsibility does not wait for an invitation.

units.title: Warning Signs and the Safety Plan Card

blocks.x: This concept teaches the general skill: what a warning sign is and what a safety plan card is for. It uses generic categories. You build your own full, working plan later in this series, in the Relapse Prevention Plan, and this concept is its foundation.
The skill and the card

SafeCare called one of its core exercises Slippery Steps. The top step is any circumstance that raises risk in general: stress, isolation, a particular caregiving arrangement. None of these is dramatic on its own. The next step down is a distinct thought about offending, which is more specific than a risky mood. The bottom step is offending itself. Every step down is harder to stop than the one before it.
Catching it early

Notice and act at the top step. One client, struggling with unwanted thoughts, was taught by another man in the group to say to himself, silently, “Stop it. It’s not your business, go away,” the moment a thought like that arrived. It sounds almost too simple. He reported that it worked, and that noticing early and interrupting early felt like relief, not restriction. It was the first control he had ever had over the thoughts.
The card

SafeCare had clients carry a card with the names and phone numbers of people to call if risk was rising. These were people who already knew what the card was for and had agreed to be on it, so he did not have to explain everything in the moment. A phone call was enough. This concept’s worksheet has you draft a short practice version. The full version, built around your own pattern, is part of the Relapse Prevention Plan.
Why this concept matters

Change happens in three steps: noticing, then choice, then action. You cannot choose without noticing first. A warning sign helps only if you catch it early enough that you still have a choice. Waiting until the bottom step removes the choice.

blocks.head: The excuse trap
blocks.x: Two habits defeat this. The first is treating early noticing as overreacting: you wait to see whether it becomes something before doing anything, and that is how the top step turns into the bottom one. The second is writing a card too vague to use, “I’ll just be stronger,” which does not tell you what to do when you need it. (Closing sentence “A warning sign you did not act on and a card too vague to act on both fail the same way.” cut: it only restates the two habits.)

blocks.x: A Circle of Safety is a network of people, not only you, who know your history and actively help make sure you are never left alone with a child unsupervised. If you built one during the programme, it has probably changed since. This concept is about rebuilding it.
Who is in it

SafeCare built these deliberately, with people from the client’s own life. One client’s employer knew his history and agreed never to leave him isolated with young people at work. Another’s community group made sure he was never alone with children while still including him in ordinary activities alongside older members. A third had family and friends who told him plainly that their friendship depended on him not reoffending, which gave the arrangement weight that polite silence would not have. None of this relied on him monitoring himself alone.
Why rebuild

Jobs end. Friendships fade. People move, have children of their own, or lose touch. A circle assembled years ago, during or just after the programme, is a circle now only if somebody has checked. New people enter your life who were never told anything, and a circle with gaps in it is not much better than no circle.
Why this concept matters

Warning Signs and the Safety Plan Card is about noticing early and acting yourself. This concept is about not relying on yourself alone. A circle that works removes the opportunity for risk to arise, so the plan does not depend on you catching every warning sign, every time, for the rest of your life.

blocks.head: The excuse trap
blocks.x: One failure is assuming a circle built once still works, without checking it again. Another is telling people just enough to look responsible, without briefing them well enough that they would know what to do. A person who vaguely knows “something happened once” is not the same as a person who knows what to watch for and has agreed to act on it.

blocks.x: SafeCare’s groups heard the same handful of self-talk patterns often enough to recognise them on sight. None of them are dramatic. Each one makes something risky sound ordinary, and each was challenged the moment it was said out loud.
The patterns the groups heard
Three patterns showed up again and again.
Blaming something else
“It was the alcohol.” Something else becomes the reason and sits in front of the decision.
Avoiding adults
“I don’t fit in with adult conversation.” “I don’t know what to say, how to be with adults.” The discomfort is real, but it becomes a reason to withdraw from adults instead of something to work on.
Turning it into a compliment

“I get on better with kids than with adults.” “I like being with the kids. I’m King of the Kids.” The pattern that raises risk gets treated as a strength to feel good about instead of something to be honest about.
Why this concept matters

In the group, someone else usually said what needed saying: “that’s bullshit.” Self-talk like this feels true from the inside. You hear it in your own voice, in your own head, with nobody else there to challenge it. This concept builds that outside voice into your own thinking, so it does not depend on a group being there to say it.
Three ways to act

You catch yourself thinking one of the three things above, and you can tell it is a pattern and not a plain fact about you. What to do next is where the three approaches this set is built from differ, and none of them is wrong.
What GLM says to do
Do not argue with the thought. Ask which of the eleven needs the thought is about, which for all three patterns above is usually community or relationships, and build a route to that need among adults. A thought has less pull once it is no longer your only account of how a need gets met.
What CBT says to do
Treat it as a claim to test, not a fact to obey. Write the thought down, set out what supports it and what does not, and write a more accurate version beside it. You can do this one alone, on paper, at any hour.
What the SafeCare book says to do
Say it out loud to somebody who will not let it stand. The correction comes from another person who has heard it before and will say so. The groups worked this way, and that is how these three patterns came to be recognised.
No study has compared these three on this problem, so the evidence does not choose for you. The GLM route is the structure Planning My Future is built on, while the CBT route is ordinary cognitive-behavioural practice, and the search line below finds its published literature. The SafeCare route is that programme’s own group practice, which is unpublished clinical material.
Which of the three can you do this week, with the people you have? If the answer is none of them, work on that first, before the self-talk itself.

blocks.head: The excuse trap
blocks.x: Two habits show up here. The first is deciding that because you have never said these exact words, none of this applies to you. The pattern underneath is what counts. The second runs the other way: treating every ordinary thought as a hidden red flag, which turns this into a source of constant anxiety instead of an occasional check. Most thoughts are just thoughts, and these three patterns are specific.

blocks.x: This concept checks one thing: where your emotional closeness, confiding and affection currently come from, and whether any of it has been coming from a child instead of an adult.
Where closeness comes from

SafeCare found, again and again, that by the end of treatment many men recognised they had more intimacy with a child in their life than with their own partner. They had confided in a child, relied on a child emotionally and taken comfort from a child’s affection, in ways that belonged with another adult. This was not always the same relationship as the offending. It was often a separate, ordinary-looking pattern that had grown in the same direction.
Building closeness

The programme’s answer went further than withdrawing from children. It was to build adult sources of closeness, deliberately, often starting from nothing. One client took up art classes and a social club for people who had experienced childhood hardship, and made progress in both. Another, a churchgoer, started going on bus trips with an older people’s group and found friendship and affection there, some of it for the first time in his life. None of this was dramatic, but all of it took effort to start.
Why this concept matters

Boundaries and Needs described the underlying pattern: a real need met at somebody else’s expense. Planning My Future’s Relationships section, later in this series, builds this out in full. This concept is the check that comes first: knowing where you stand before trying to change it.

blocks.head: The excuse trap
blocks.x: Two habits show up here. The first is mistaking a child’s easy, uncomplicated affection for adult closeness, and treating that substitution as harmless because it feels similar from the inside. The substitution is not harmless, and the similar feeling is the problem. The second is the avoiding-adults pattern from What People Tell Themselves showing up again here, “I’m just not good with adults,” used as a reason not to try building anything new. Both leave the gap where it is.

The worksheet for this concept has six review boxes by design, and you will live a great deal longer than six years.

Building My Protective Factors, directly after this one, is the other half of this pair. This concept leaves a gap, and the next one answers it.
Three tiers of risk factors

Researchers group risk factors into three kinds. Static factors, your age, your criminal history, the number and type of your victims, whether you have ever lived with a partner for two years, are used to work out a starting risk level. None of them can change, whatever effort you put in, and this concept only asks you to know they exist.

Stable dynamic factors are things about how you live and think that endure for months or years and that can change with sustained effort. Treatment works on these, and they are the main subject of this concept.
Acute dynamic factors shift over days or weeks and signal that risk is rising right now. This concept covers these too, more briefly, since they are what you watch week to week.
Your history is closed. Your present is not, and everything that follows is about your present.

blocks.head: Why there is no score
blocks.x: The instrument behind this list is normally scored by a trained assessor, working from a coding manual, a structured interview and a file review, after two days of training. How closely a man’s own scoring would match an assessor’s has never been measured, and the match would likely be poor. A low self-score gives false reassurance. A high one causes distress and offers no way to act on it, especially on an item like deviant sexual interests, which your offence history keeps high however hard you try. This concept asks what you recognise, in your own words, and links each factor to a need in Planning My Future. It never asks for a number. Checking yourself against this list more than occasionally is rumination. Noticing a factor is information.
The fifteen factors
Grouped as your own programme taught them. Each points to a need this series’ companion workbook, Planning My Future, already works on.
Who is around you
1. Significant social influences.

The people in your life who are not paid to be there, and the balance between how many pull you toward a decent life and how many pull the other way. Three good mates and nobody else beats fifteen contacts who all pull the wrong direction.
Points to: Community, Relatedness.
How you do closeness
2. Capacity for relationship stability.

Whether you have ever managed to live with an adult partner for a couple of years, and whether your relationships tend to hold together or come apart. The item measures capacity, not current status, so being single right now is not the issue.
Points to: Relatedness.
3. Emotional identification with children.

Feeling more comfortable, more understood, more yourself around children than around adults. Describing a child as a friend or a confidant. This item is one of the better-supported on the list, and it is scored only for men whose victim was thirteen or under.
Points to: Relatedness, Community.
4. Hostility toward women.
Carrying anger, suspicion or contempt toward women as a group. Believing they are deceitful, or that they have it easy, or that they are the reason things went wrong for you.
Points to: Relatedness, Inner peace.
5. General social rejection and loneliness.
Feeling on the outside of everything. Not necessarily alone in a room, but not feeling you belong anywhere.
Points to: Community, Relatedness.
6. Lack of concern for others.
Not registering how what you do affects other people, or registering it and finding it does not weigh much.
Points to: Relatedness, Spirituality.
How you handle sex
7. Sex drive and sexual preoccupation.
How much room sex takes up in your head, hours a day thinking about it, planning it, looking for it. The item concerns volume, not content.
Points to: Inner peace, Happiness.
8. Sex as coping.
Turning to sex, masturbation or pornography to manage a feeling instead of to enjoy yourself. Bored, lonely, angry, humiliated, anxious, and the reliable answer is sex.
Points to: Inner peace, Happiness.
9. Deviant sexual interests.

What you are aroused by. Assessors score this partly from what you say, partly from testing, and partly from your offence history, which means you cannot lower it by reporting it differently. This is the item most likely to cause distress and least suited to working through alone. If it raises something urgent, talk to your psychologist, a GP or the mental health line for your state or territory, instead of trying to resolve it on the page.
Points to: a professional conversation, not a need in the workbook.
Beliefs about sex and people
10. Sexual entitlement.
Believing your sexual needs come first, that you are owed sex, or that going without is an injustice being done to you.
Points to: Relatedness, Excellence in agency.
11. Rape attitudes.
Beliefs that excuse or minimise forced sex with adults.
Points to: Relatedness.
How you handle being supervised
12. Co-operation with supervision.

Whether you keep to your conditions, and beyond that whether you work with the people supervising you or work around them. Turning up and saying nothing scores worse than turning up and being difficult but honest.
Points to: Excellence in agency.
How you run yourself
13. Impulsive acts.
Acting first and thinking afterwards, across your life generally, not only where it touches offending.
Points to: Excellence in agency, Inner peace.
14. Poor problem-solving.
Getting stuck when a problem arrives. Freezing, avoiding, or taking the first answer available.
Points to: Knowledge, Excellence in agency.
15. Negative emotionality and hostility.
How often you sit in anger, resentment or grievance, and how long it takes you to come out of it.
Points to: Inner peace.
The seven acute factors

These change over days or weeks, not months or years, which makes them the ones to watch. Four are most closely linked to reoffending: access to victims or potential victims, sexual preoccupations, rejection of supervision, and hostility. The other three still matter.
1. Access to victims or potential victims
2. Emotional collapse
3. Collapse of social supports
4. Hostility
5. Substance abuse
6. Sexual preoccupations
7. Rejection of supervision
In the original research, one bad week on its own did not predict much, and averaging these over six months predicted better than any single rating.
Limits of this list
Numbers describe groups

Every factor here was identified by comparing large groups of men who reoffended against large groups who did not. This list does not tell you what you will do. Men with several of these factors mostly do not reoffend, and men with none of them sometimes do.
Weak individual items

The list works better as a whole than any single part does alone. Emotional identification with children, on its own, barely separated reoffenders from non-reoffenders in the original research, though men who scored highest on it did reoffend at markedly higher rates. A later, larger analysis found every item in the shorter, current version predicted significantly. Both findings are true, and they do not fit together neatly.
Items later dropped

The original instrument had three attitude items: sexual entitlement, rape attitudes, and beliefs supportive of adult-child sex. None of the three predicted sexual reoffending, and all three were later dropped from the current version. Your own programme had already left the third out. This does not mean attitudes do not matter. It means researchers have not found a way to measure them that predicts reoffending.
Built for community supervision

It was designed to be scored by officers supervising men living in the community, and it was not built with online offending specifically in mind. If your offending was online, some items, especially access to potential victims, mean something different for you than the manual assumes.
A snapshot in time
It describes roughly the next six to twelve months. It does not describe your character permanently, and nor does anything else on this page.

blocks.x: Understanding My Risk Factors told you what to stop, and that is half of it. A man with no pro-offending friends has removed a risk, but he has not gained a decent social network. He may have nobody at all. This concept is about building the second half, and its research is the strongest evidence in this series for why Planning My Future, the workbook that follows this book, exists.

Keep two findings in mind through the rest of this concept. First, up to half of men assessed as high risk on every static and dynamic measure do not sexually reoffend, even when followed for more than twenty years. This module exists because researchers went looking for what was different about them. Second, risk falls with time spent offence-free in the community, and most reoffending happens in the first five years. A man who has kept a decent life going for a decade is at lower risk than he was when he walked out the gate.

blocks.x: No numbers here either, for the same reasons as in Understanding My Risk Factors, plus one more specific to this instrument. Even trained assessors only moderately agree with each other on the Adaptive Sexuality items, which are also the items most closely tied to sexual reoffending. If trained professionals struggle to rate these consistently, a self-rating has no value as a number. Written as a plain word with an example, it tells you something.
The fourteen factors
Grouped by what they describe. Each points to a need in Planning My Future, the same as the risk factors did.
Resilience
1. Adaptive schemas.

Beliefs about yourself and other people that hold up under pressure. Thinking of yourself as someone with worth without needing that constantly confirmed, and thinking of other people as reasonably trustworthy without being naive about it.
Points to: Inner peace.
2. Empathy.
Registering what is going on for another person and being moved by it. The item asks whether you do this in practice.
Points to: Relatedness.
3. Coping.
Having ways of getting through difficulty that work and that do not cost you or anyone else. Have more than one: if your only coping strategy fails, you are left without one.
Points to: Inner peace.
4. Self-control.
Being able to hold off on something you want. In the American validation study this was the single strongest predictor of getting through supervision without a sexual offence.
Points to: Excellence in agency.
5. Attitudes towards rules and regulations.
Accepting that rules apply to you, including ones you think are stupid. The item concerns your general stance, not compliance with any one particular condition.
Points to: Community, Excellence in agency.
Adaptive sexuality
This set of items is what makes this instrument different from every other protective factors measure, and it is the set that predicted sexual reoffending specifically.
6. Sexual self-regulation.
Being able to manage sexual urges, with a sex drive that sits in a normal range rather than dominating your week.
Points to: Inner peace, Happiness.
7. Prosocial sexual interests.
Being interested in, and aroused by, sex with consenting adults. This item asks what is present, not what is absent.
Points to: Relatedness, Happiness.
8. Prosocial sexual identity.
Having accepted a way of seeing yourself sexually that is adult, lawful and liveable. Being able to answer who you are sexually with something other than what you did.
Points to: Relatedness, Spirituality.
9. Intimate relationship.
A romantic and physical relationship of reasonable quality and stability.
Points to: Relatedness.
Prosocial connection and reward
10. Goal-directed living.
Having things you are working towards, and organising your time around them.
Points to: Spirituality, Excellence in agency.
11. Work.
Paid or unpaid, so long as it is real and regular.
Points to: Excellence in work.
12. Leisure activities.
Things you do because you want to, that give you something back.
Points to: Excellence in play, Creativity.
13. Social network.
People around you who are not offending, and who know you.
Points to: Community.
14. Emotional connection to adults.
At least one adult you can be honest with. In the American study this was the item most often missing from the record, and its absence separated the men who got revoked from the men who did not.
Points to: Relatedness.

A fourth group of six items exists in the full instrument, covering professional supervision and treatment structures. Those belong to the people managing your case, not to you directly, so they are not included here.
Two needs with nothing here

Life, meaning physical health, and Knowledge, meaning learning, have no matching item anywhere in this instrument, which is a gap in the instrument and not an omission on this page. Research has not yet established that looking after your body or continuing to learn reduces sexual reoffending specifically. Planning My Future still asks about both, because a good life includes them, but this concept covers a narrower question than a good life.
What the evidence shows
Two validation studies exist, and they do not agree about how large the effect is.

A New Zealand study of 210 men, followed for over twelve years on average, found that protective factor scores strongly predicted staying free of sexual reoffending, a large effect, and the result held even after accounting for static risk. An American study of 170 men under close post-release supervision found a much smaller overall effect, though self-control and coping specifically still predicted well on their own.

In that American sample, the standard static risk instrument predicted nothing. The protective factors measure outperformed it. A reader with a static risk number he cannot change can see from this that protective factors can predict outcomes where the static number did not.

The complicating finding: the relationship was not a straight line. Below a certain overall level, having some protective factors showed no measurable benefit. Above that level, the outcomes improved sharply. Partial protection did not appear to protect. This suggests building depth in a few areas over a thin layer spread across all fourteen.
Limits of this list
Newer evidence

This instrument is only a few years old and has been validated twice, in two countries, with results that differ in size. Understanding My Risk Factors rests on twenty years of accumulated data. This concept does not. Treat what follows as promising but unconfirmed.
Why the studies differ

The likeliest explanation is the setting. Men held under close post-release supervision cannot easily work, form relationships, or build a social network, so the items measuring those things had less room to show anything. This reflects the conditions, not the men.
Factors outside your control

Work, a social network and an intimate relationship all depend on other people agreeing to have you. Social attitudes and the practical conditions of life after a conviction can make some of these hard to build. Such difficulty is an obstacle, not a personal failing. Build what is available to you, and do not conclude that nothing is.
Below the halfway mark
The study that looked closely found no measurable benefit below the halfway mark.
No guarantees

The same as last time, in reverse. Protective factors describe groups. Men with many of them sometimes still reoffend. This concept and the one before it are both about probabilities, not certainties, and neither one is a verdict on any single person.

blocks.x: This workbook is yours
This workbook is here to help you build a plan for the life you want, rather than the life somebody else thinks you ought to want. It belongs to you, and it only works if what goes in it is true.

You will not finish it in one sitting, and it was never designed for that. Plan on working through it over several weeks, one section at a time, and consider talking it over with somebody as you go. Some sections will take you ten minutes. Others will sit in the back of your head for a few days before you write anything down, and that is how it is meant to go.
This workbook is not marked, and there is no pass or fail. A short, true answer helps you more than a long one written to look good for whoever might read it.

This workbook is not tied to a programme. You might be writing in it during a treatment group, or years afterwards with nobody looking over your shoulder, or somewhere in between with a psychologist you found yourself. The workbook works in all three, so some parts say things like if you are working through this with somebody. If you are not, that part is simply not for you, and you carry on.

blocks.head: Before you start
blocks.x: Be clear about all of this before you write anything at all.
If you are working through this with a psychologist or a counsellor, they will read what you write, because that is how they can help you with it.
Nobody else reads it unless you choose to show them.
Your saved file is stored somewhere, either on a service system or on your own computer or phone. Know which, and know who else can get at that device.
In some situations, documents like this one can be requested by other agencies. That stays true years after you write it.

So write honestly about what you thought, felt and wanted, because that is what this work deals with. You do not need to write out details of what you did. If you are ever unsure whether something belongs in here, leave it out. If there is somebody you can ask, ask them first, and treat that conversation as part of the work.
The idea behind this workbook
This workbook is built on something called the Good Lives Model. The name sounds more formal than the idea, which is straightforward.

People want a handful of basic things: feeling well, feeling calm, feeling close to somebody, feeling like they are good at something, and feeling like their life adds up to something. Nobody has to be taught to want any of that. Those things are called fundamental needs, and there are eleven of them in this workbook.

Offending can be an attempt to meet one of those ordinary needs, and if it was, the need itself was never the problem. Wanting to feel calm is not a problem, and wanting to feel wanted is not a problem either. The problem was the route taken to get there, because that route harmed another person and badly damaged your own life as well.
The need stays. The route has to change.

In this workbook you work out which of the eleven needs matter most to you and how well each one is being met now. You also work out which of them were tangled up in your offending and what you are going to do differently from here. Be specific: put days and names on it.
The companion workbook

A second book goes with this one, called Understanding My Past. It comes out of the SafeCare programme, which ran in Western Australia for about twenty years and worked with around 700 families. If you have not been given a copy, ask whoever gave you this one.
The two books do different jobs.
Understanding My Past asks how you got here, and what you need to keep an eye on.
This workbook asks what you are building instead.
Reading that one first, or at least being partway through it, makes this one easier, because it is hard to plan a life when you have not yet worked out what went wrong in the one you had.
Why the books differ

If you read both, you will notice they do not tell the same story about why offending happens. This workbook says that offending is an ordinary need met by a harmful route. The other book says that the part of you that offended was the child in you who never got to finish growing up, acting out in a grown man’s body. Those are two different explanations, and this set does not treat them as one.

They fit together better than they look. The SafeCare model describes three parts of a person. The Pseudo Adult is the grown-up front you learned to put on. The Inner Child is the part of you that got stuck at the age when something happened that you could not handle. The True Adult’s job is to act as umpire between the other two, permanently. Concept 6 of Understanding My Past, Pseudo Adult, Inner Child, True Adult, explains that model in full. Here there is only enough of it to make the next part make sense.
Those eleven needs belong to that part of you as well.

So when this workbook asks how well you are meeting the need for closeness, or calm, or being good at something, it is asking about the adult you show the world. It is also asking about the part of you that never got those things and still wants them. Meeting those needs openly, as an adult, is how you look after that part of yourself. When they stay unmet, that part comes out in ways you do not choose.
Understanding My Past shows you who is asking. This workbook is where you work out how to answer without hurting anybody.
Goals to work towards
Plans that consist only of things to avoid tend to fall over, and there are two reasons for that.
The first is that a rule like “do not think about it” gives your brain nothing at all to do except think about it. If you doubt that, try not thinking about your left hand for the next ten seconds.

The second reason is that avoiding something always leaves a hole where it used to be. If the behaviour was how you switched off at the end of a bad day, and you take it away without putting anything in its place, you still have the bad day. Now you have nothing to do with it. That gap is where a plan can come unstuck, and it can happen months later, once everybody around you has relaxed.

So this workbook asks you for approach goals, which are things you are going to do. You will still have some firm rules about what you stay well away from, and you keep them, but a set of rules is not a life. The plan fills the space the rules leave empty.
Compare these two
I will stop being on my own so much.
I will ring my brother every Sunday afternoon, and I will go to the Thursday night darts at the club starting from the first week of next month.
Both of those come from the same intention, but only one of them tells you what you are supposed to be doing on Sunday.

The needs overlap, which is normal and not a sign you have misunderstood something. Playing in a band could sit under play, creativity, community and relationships. This is perfectly fine! Write it wherever it fits best.
Four plan faults
A plan can go wrong in four main ways, and knowing about them now will save you rewriting a good deal of your plan later on.
Harmful route
A step in the plan does meet a need, but it hurts somebody else in the process, or it puts you somewhere you have no business being. The need was fine and the route was not.
Too narrow
The plan covers two or three needs properly and leaves out all the rest. It holds up until something knocks out one of those two or three, and then the plan has no other support.
Conflicting goals

Working sixty-hour weeks and being present for your kids are both good things to want, but together they are impossible. Something has to give, and if you have not decided in advance what it will be, life will decide for you.
Missing resources
The step needs a skill, some money, transport, a licence or an opportunity that you do not have yet. That does not make it a bad goal. It makes it a goal that is missing its first step.
A later section covers checking your plan against these four faults. Read it before you get too far in. Read the section on checking your plan
Working on screen or paper

You can work through this on screen or on paper, and both give you the same plan. The boxes to tick and the options to circle in this workbook can be filled in on screen. Your written answers go in My Journal, which comes in a version you fill in on screen and a version you print. A few practical points before you start.
On screen, use Adobe Acrobat Reader, which is free and works on a computer, a phone or a tablet. Other apps may look like they are working and then fail to save your answers properly.
On screen, save the file onto your own device as soon as you start, and save it again at the end of every session, because the file does not save by itself.
On paper, print the pages you need and keep them together in one folder. A pencil is useful for anything you expect to change.
You can leave any box empty and return to it whenever you like, because no box locks once you have moved past it.

If writing or typing is a hassle for you, or if reading is hard work, say so early instead of struggling on. Somebody can go through it with you out loud while you write short notes, and that is a normal way to do this. On your own, use whatever your phone or computer offers for reading text aloud, or talk your answer into a voice recorder first and write it down afterwards.
Put the date on everything. On screen, give your file a name you will still recognise in three months, with the date somewhere in it. On paper, write the date at the top of each page you fill in.

Your review dates
A plan that you write once and never open again is only a piece of writing. It starts working as a plan when you review it.

Things change, often faster than you expect. You will finish a goal, a job will end, somebody will move away, and a step that made perfect sense in winter will make no sense at all by summer. If the plan does not change along with all of that, it slowly stops describing your life, and once that happens you stop trusting it and stop opening it.

So pick your first review date now, before you have written anything else in here. Somewhere between six weeks and three months from today is about right for a first review. Put it in your phone while you are thinking about it rather than telling yourself you will do it later.
How to do a review
1.	Get out your most recent copy, whether that is the saved file or the printed pages.

2.	Make a fresh copy before you change anything, and keep the old one, because you can look back later and see how far you have come. On screen, save it straight away under a new name with today’s date in it. On paper, print fresh pages or copy the old ones, and date them.

3.	Work through the new copy and change anything that has gone out of date. On screen, just type over the top of it. On paper, put a single line through the old answer and write the new one beside it.
4.	Look hardest at the ratings. If a score has dropped, treat it as information, not a failure, because you have it early enough to act on.
5.	Set the next review date before you put the plan away, rather than after.
When to review early
A big change of any kind, such as a relationship ending, a move, a new job, losing a job, a death in the family, or a health scare.
Any of the warning signs you wrote into your plan turning up.
You notice that you have stopped opening the plan at all, which is easy to miss because there is no particular moment when it happens.
When is your first review? Write the date.
When is your second review? Write the date.
When is your third review? Write the date.
Sharing your plan
Pick at least one person who is going to see your plan.

Sharing the plan is not a formality, and it is not about being checked up on. A plan that exists only inside your own head is easy to drop, and nobody notices when you do, including you. A plan that somebody else has read is harder to drop. That person can ask how the Sunday phone calls are going, or say that you have gone quiet lately and ask what is going on. They may also notice one of your warning signs before you are willing to admit to it yourself.

Choose somebody who is steady, who you will realistically still be talking to in six months, and who can hear something uncomfortable without either falling apart or going off at you. The bar is higher than it sounds, so think it through instead of picking whoever is nearest. It might be a brother, a mate, a partner, your GP, a counsellor or a support worker.

You do not have to hand over all of it either. You might share one section, or just your warning signs along with what you would like them to do if they spot one. Work out what you are sharing before you sit down with them, and tell them plainly what you want from them, because a person who wants to help may not know how.

The person I will share this with is __________, and I chose them because __________.
What I want them to do is __________, and what I do not want them to do is __________.
I will ask them on __________, and I will start by saying __________.
Who will you share your plan with? Write their name.
How do you know that person?
What will you share with them, and what do you want them to do?
What date will you ask them?
What date did you share it? Fill this in once you have.
