Go to How to Use This Workbook

Every one of the eleven need sections is laid out the same way, so once you have been through the first one you will know your way around the rest. What changes between sections is the kind of question you are asked, because asking the same question eleven times produces eleven identical answers that nobody believes.
How each need section works

Every section opens with an explanation of what that need means, followed by two short lists showing what it looks like when it is going well and when it is not. A panel then explains why that particular need matters for someone in your position. After that come eight boxes for you to fill in, and each box has a heading, a short explanation of what it is asking for, a prompt to help you get started, and a space to write.

Work through the eight boxes in order rather than jumping around, because several of them build on the ones before. A sensible warning sign in box 6 is very hard to write if you have not yet worked out in box 2 why the need matters to you at all.
The eight boxes
1. Rate your ability

A number from 0 to 10 showing how well this need is being met in your life at the moment. A high number is not the aim. The number lets you see at a glance which areas need attention first, and gives you something to compare against at your next review.
2. Why this matters to me

This box asks what the need means in your own life. A plan built on things you think you are supposed to care about tends to give way the first time it is tested, because nothing is behind it. Use this box to work out what is behind it.
3. This need and my offending

Some needs will have been tangled up in your offending and some will not, and either answer is fine. This box asks about the state you were in, what you were feeling and what you were chasing, rather than about the behaviour itself. Answering truthfully here shows you where the repair work needs to go.
4. Steps to meet this need
The practical part, and the one that changes your week. These are things you are going to do, written down specifically enough that somebody else could tell whether you had done them or not.
5. Signs of success
How you will know it is working. Progress in these areas is slow and easy to miss, and if you cannot see yourself getting anywhere you may stop trying, so do not skip this box.
6. Signs of concern
Your early warnings. The aim is to spot a slide in the first week rather than the eighth, because by the eighth week it has usually taken a few other things down with it.
7. Response to concern
What you will do when a warning sign shows up, decided now while things are steady. On the day you need this, you will not be in a state to think one up from scratch, so write it in advance.
8. Progress, changes and support
Left mostly empty at first and filled in at each review. This box turns the workbook from something you wrote once into a record of what has happened since.
The different kinds of prompt

The prompts change from section to section, partly to stop it turning into a form-filling exercise and partly because different questions suit different needs. Here is what each kind is for, so you can recognise them when they turn up.
Questions to think about

A short list of questions coming at the same thing from different angles. You are not meant to answer all of them. Pick the two or three that start you thinking and answer those in full, then leave the rest alone.
Sentence starters

A line with gaps in it, such as “When I feel __________, what I usually do is __________”. You do not write in the gaps on the page: read the sentence, work out how you would finish it, then write the full sentence in the box underneath. The gaps give you a frame for your answer when you are not sure how to start.
Check your answer

A short checklist that you apply to your own answer after you have written it. Write first, then read your answer back against the list and fix whatever fails. It works like a tradesman checking his own work before somebody else sees it.
Word banks

A run of single words separated by slashes, covering the ground that a need takes in. Use them to jog your memory about areas you might not have considered. Never write the words down as your answer, because on their own they are far too vague for anybody to act on.
Notes
Short asides that flag a common mistake in that box. Read them, because they will usually save you writing something you have to redo later.
Worked examples

A few sections include an example written by somebody else, set deliberately on its own separate page rather than next to the box. Read it once to see the level you are aiming for, then go back and write your own from scratch. If your answer ends up looking like the example, then you have written somebody else’s plan instead of your own, and it will not hold up when you need it to.
Using it well
A few habits make this more useful.
Write it in your own words, including the awkward ones. Language borrowed from group, from a court report or from a book you half remember will sound fine and mean nothing to you in six months.
Be specific about everything: names, days, times and places. “Regularly” and “more often” are intentions with the useful part left out.
Do not save the hard sections for later, because later often does not arrive. If a section is uncomfortable, that is usually a sign it is one you most need to do.
If you have a group or someone you trust, take it to them. The sections get better once somebody else has asked you a question about them.
Do not aim for a workbook that looks impressive. Aim for one that would still make sense to you on your worst week of the year, because that is the week you will be reading it.
Help with reading and writing

This part can be difficult, whatever you have to say. If you have a psychologist, tell them early instead of pushing through and ending up with a workbook full of one-line answers that do not help you. Short honest answers are fine, and you can return to a box later.
Someone you trust can read the sections out to you and write what you say.
You can answer out loud and type up short notes afterwards, or record yourself and work from that.
You can pair up with someone you trust, with one of you asking the questions and the other answering, and then swap over.
Short answers are fine. Six honest words beat six polished lines that you copied from somewhere.
Where to start

Start at the beginning with Life, and go through the eleven needs in order. They are arranged so that the more concrete ones come before the ones that take more thinking, and by the time you reach the harder sections you will have had some practice.
Go to Step 1, getting started Go straight to the first need, Life

Life means being well in your body and your mind, and it is the plainest need on the list. It covers the ordinary maintenance of being a person: sleeping, eating, moving your body, whatever you drink or take, going to the doctor when something is wrong, and feeling reasonably alright in your own skin.

Life sits first because it is the base the other needs depend on, so when it gives way the rest tend to go with it. Poor sleep alone will flatten your mood, shorten your temper and make it hard to concentrate. It also makes every other need in this workbook harder to meet, because you cannot think your way out of being exhausted.

This need covers more than the physical side of things. It also covers how you feel about your body and your health, which is not the same as what the numbers say. Two men with identical blood pressure can feel completely differently about themselves. Write about both here.
Signs of progress
You sleep most nights, and you wake up feeling rested.
You eat at roughly normal times on most days, without having to think about it much.
Your body moves regularly in some way, and that does not have to mean a gym, because walking counts.
Alcohol and anything else you use do not decide how your evenings go.
You go to the doctor when something is wrong, rather than waiting several months to see whether it gets worse on its own.
You do not particularly dread what you see in the mirror.
Signs of drifting
You are up half the night and flat all the following day, and each of those two things keeps feeding the other.
You eat whatever happens to be nearest, or you barely eat at all, or you eat mainly because you are bored.
Weeks go past without you leaving the house for any reason that was not compulsory.
You drink to get yourself off to sleep, or to stop yourself thinking about something.
You have a pain or symptom that you have decided to ignore, sometimes for years.
If one line in those two lists described you, keep it in mind while you work through the boxes below.
Why this need matters

Poor sleep, low mood and a body that has stopped being looked after do not cause anybody to offend, and plenty of exhausted, unwell people never harm anyone at all. What those things do is wear down the part of you that stops and thinks before acting. The decisions you make at two in the morning, tired and flat and on your own, are not the ones you would make at ten on a Saturday after a walk and a decent night’s sleep. Look back for a stretch where your health fell apart before things went wrong. Knowing that about yourself is not an excuse. It is a pattern you can learn to watch for.

Eight boxes follow. Each gives you a different way into the question, so they will not feel the same. Some ask you to finish a sentence, some ask you to test what you have already written, and some ask a question from an unusual angle. Work through them in order.
1. Rate your ability
Before you pick a number, decide what the numbers mean to you, because a 6 has no meaning until you know what your own 10 would look like.
Set your own scale first
Write these three in your own words, and keep them realistic. A 10 is not perfect health or the body you had at twenty-two, but the best this could be for you, at your age, with the life you have.
Describe what a 0 for Life looks like for you, in your own words.
Describe what a 5 for Life looks like for you.
Describe what a 10 for Life looks like for you. Not perfect health, just the best this could be at your age.
Rate where you are today
Rate Life as it stands today, 0 to 10, where 0 means the need is not met at all and 10 means it is fully met.
A low number here is information. Low scores tell you where the work needs to start. A page full of 8s and 9s often means the person has not looked hard yet.
2. Why this matters to me

The question is not why health matters in general, because everybody already knows that sleep is good for them and that knowledge has never changed anyone’s behaviour on its own. The question is why it matters to you, in the life you are living this year.
Questions to think about
Pick whichever two or three of these questions get something moving in your head, answer those ones properly, and ignore the rest without feeling bad about it.
Describe a good Tuesday, not a holiday or a birthday, just an ordinary Tuesday where your body and your head both felt right. What was in that day?
What could you do at twenty-five that you cannot do now, and does losing that bother you, or have you made your peace with it?
Who else is affected when your health starts to slide, and which of them notices it before you do?
If a doctor gave you one piece of news next week that made you change something immediately, what would that news have to be?
What would “enough” look like in this area? Not the ideal version of it, just enough to be going on with.
3. This need and my offending

For some men the answer to this is no, and no is a complete answer. For others there is a clear link, and this is the place to write it. Either way, this box asks about the state you were in, not about the behaviour itself, so write about what was going on in your body and your head in the lead up to it.
Write about how you felt, what you wanted and what you were thinking at the time. Do not describe the offending.
Sentence starters
In the months before things went wrong, my sleep was __________ and my drinking was __________.
Physically I felt __________ on most days, and looking back at it now, the first thing that started to slide was __________.
When I was feeling like that, what I wanted was __________.
The behaviour gave me __________, which I was not getting anywhere else in my life at that point.
If my health had been in better shape back then, what might have been different is __________.
Was your offending motivated by the Life need? Write what you wanted and how you felt at the time, not what you did.

Writing down a link here is not making an excuse, and being tired or unwell does not make anyone offend. The link shows you where the repair work needs to start, because a plan that ignores the state you were in has no foundation. See how one man answered this box
4. Steps to meet this need
This box changes what your week looks like. Everything before it is thinking, and this part is doing.
Pick your area
Pick two or three of the areas below that matter to you. Do not write those words down as your answer, because on their own they are too vague to act on.
sleep / alcohol / walking / food / water / screens at night / GP / dentist / medication / teeth / weight / smoking / back / knees / hearing / eyes / daylight / routine / caffeine / mornings
Make each a weekly action
Every step you write needs to have four things in it. Write your steps out first, then read them back against this list and fix any that fail.
a.	A what, meaning the actual action rather than the outcome you are hoping for, so “walk” rather than “get fitter”.
b.	A when, meaning a day or a time you could put in your phone, so “each morning before work” or “Tuesday and Thursday”, rather than “regularly”.
c.	A where or who, meaning a place or a person’s name, because a step with neither tends to stay theoretical.
d.	Something you will do rather than something you will stop, and if you have written a stopping step, add the thing that is going to fill the space it leaves behind.
Aim for two or three steps. Three steps you carry out will do more for you than ten you read once and never look at again.
Write two or three steps for Life. Each one needs a what, a when, and a where or a who, and each has to be something you will do rather than something you will stop.
5. Signs of success
How will you know that any of this is working? Decide that now, because progress you cannot see is easy to stop working on.
Ask it from outside yourself

You are a poor judge of your own gradual improvement, because you are with yourself every day and the change is too slow to see up close. Other people are much better at spotting it, so answer these as though you were them.
Think of someone who sees you every week. What would they notice first, and would they say something about it or just think it?
Think of someone who knows you well, such as your psychologist, three months from now. What would have to be different for them to say that this one has shifted?
Think of yourself in six months looking back at today. What is the small, unglamorous thing you would tell yourself to keep doing?

Be wary of signs that only exist inside your own head, such as “feeling more positive about things”, because nobody else can see those and neither can you on a bad day. Look instead for things that could be noticed from the outside.
6. Signs of concern
These are your early warnings. Write them down so you catch a slide in week one, not week eight, when it is much harder to pull back from.
Trace back a bad stretch
Think of a stretch when your health fell away badly, whether or not it had anything to do with your offending, and then run that period backwards rather than forwards.
Once it was clearly bad and you could not pretend otherwise, what was happening in your days?
Two weeks before that point, what had already changed? Look for something small and specific rather than anything dramatic.
What was the first thing to go? It may be one dropped routine rather than any particular event.
Did anyone say anything to you at the time, and if they did, what did you tell them?
That first thing to go is your warning sign. Write it as something you could check. “Three nights in a row where I did not get to sleep before two” can be checked, and “feeling a bit off” cannot.
7. Response to concern
Write this one now, while things are steady. It belongs in the plan because you will not be in a state to invent a response on the day you need one.
Build it as if-then
An if-then plan works because the decision is already made, so there is nothing left to talk yourself out of when the moment arrives.
If I notice __________, then within __________ I will __________.
The person I will tell is __________, and I will tell them by __________ (a text, a phone call, or in person).
If I cannot get hold of them, my second person is __________.
The excuse I am most likely to use for not doing any of this is __________, and my answer to that excuse is __________.
Spend the longest on that last stem. You probably have a standard excuse that you use without noticing, and writing it down now takes most of its power away.
What will you do when you notice that first warning sign for Life? Write one response for the first sign and a faster one if it keeps going.
8. Progress, changes and support
Fill in the first part of this box now, and return to it at every review. The workbook stops being a document you wrote once and becomes a record of what happened.
Build on what worked
You are not starting from zero here, even if it feels that way at the moment.
Give one occasion in the last month when this need was met even slightly, whether that was one decent night’s sleep, one walk, or one day where you ate properly.
What made that possible? Think about where you were, what time it was, who else was involved and what was different about that particular day.
What would it take to make that happen twice as often? The answer may be smaller and more boring than you expect.
Review questions
What has improved since the last review? Be specific, and be fair to yourself.
Which step did not happen? Work out whether it was the wrong step or just the wrong week, because those two problems have very different solutions.
What support do you need that you are not currently getting, who could provide it, and have you asked them yet?
Final check
Every box has something in it, even if what you have written is short.
Each of your steps has a what, a when, and either a where or a who.
At least one of those steps is something you could start this week rather than next month.
Your response to concern gives a person’s name, not “someone” or “my support network”.
Nothing you have written could harm another person or put you at risk of offending. Checking Your Plan

blocks.x: This need is about being free of stress and emotional turmoil, and being able to sit still in your own company without something churning away underneath. It covers stress, worry, anger, guilt and shame, and it also covers whether you have any reliable way of settling yourself down when those things turn up.

Everyone has difficult feelings, and this need does not ask you to be calm all the time. It asks whether the difficult feelings pass through when they arrive instead of staying, and whether you have something to do with them other than swallowing them or acting on them.

It also covers feeling safe, both physically and in the sense of not spending your days braced for the next thing to go wrong. You may look calm from the outside and still live with a background tension you have got used to, to the point where you no longer notice it and would not know what its absence felt like.
Signs of progress
You can sit on your own for an hour without needing something to distract you from your own head.
When something goes wrong, you feel it and then it passes, rather than lingering for a fortnight.
You have two or three things you can reliably do that bring you back down, and you do them.
You can tell somebody that you are struggling before it reaches the point of a crisis.
You are not lying awake running arguments you have already had.
Signs of drifting
You are tense most of the time without being able to point at a particular reason for it.
Small things set you off, and afterwards you cannot explain the size of the reaction, even to yourself.
You need something on in the background at all times, because silence is uncomfortable.
Feelings get pushed down and stored rather than dealt with, until something eventually knocks the lid off.
Your only reliable way of switching off is something you would rather other people did not know about.
That last line is the reason this need sits so early in the workbook. Stop on it for a moment before you go on.
Why this need matters

Think back to any stress or emptiness you had no idea how to shift, and whether a behaviour switched it off completely for a couple of hours. If it did, it was chosen less because it was appealing than because it worked, quickly and reliably, in a life where nothing else did. If you take away the one thing that worked without replacing it, the problem is still there. You have made the pressure worse and removed the valve.
Eight boxes again, and the prompts in this section are different from the ones in Life. Work through them in order.
1. Rate your ability
This one moves around more than most, so a single number for today does not tell you very much on its own. Rate it at three points instead, and pay attention to the difference between them.
Rate three points in time
Rate Inner peace as it was about a year ago, 0 to 10.
Rate Inner peace as it was about a month ago, 0 to 10.
Rate Inner peace as it stands today, 0 to 10.
Now explain the gaps
If those three numbers are different from each other, something changed them, and knowing what changed them tells you more than the numbers do.
If those three numbers are different from each other, what changed between them?
If all three numbers came out the same, check whether that is true or whether you picked a number and stuck with it. A year is a long time for nothing to change.
2. Why this matters to me
Do not stop at describing what stress feels like, which everybody already knows. Write about what it costs you and what it gets in the way of.
Sentence starters
When I am wound up, the first person to cop it is __________, and what they get from me is __________.
The thing I stop doing when I am stressed is __________.
If I had one settled month, the thing I would finally get around to is __________.
I have been carrying __________ for about __________ years now.
What I want here is not to feel nothing but __________.
Why does Inner peace matter to you? Write what you want here, even if it is different from what you think you should want.
3. This need and my offending
You may answer yes to this, and see that your offending hinged on it. Take your time over this box.
Write about what you were feeling, what you wanted and what you were trying to get away from. Do not describe the offending.
Questions to think about
Pick the two or three of these that get something moving, and answer those properly.
What was the feeling you were trying to get away from? Give it a name, even a clumsy one, and be more precise than “stressed” if you can.
How long did the relief last afterwards, and what did the hour after that feel like?
What else had you tried before this, and why did those things not work or not last?
Was it about feeling something, or about feeling nothing for a while? Those are two different things and they lead to different plans.
If somebody had asked you at the time whether you were stressed, what would you have told them?

Understanding that a behaviour worked as a way of coping is not excusing it, and it does not make it any less harmful to the people affected by it. It tells you what your plan has to replace, and a plan that does not replace it will not last. See how one man answered this box
4. Steps to meet this need

The trap in this box is writing down five or six calming things you have heard of and never done, and then doing none of them. What you need here is a very small number of things you will use on a bad day.
List more than you need
Write six things that might settle you down. Include the obvious ones and the daft ones, and do not filter anything out yet.
Rank them

Now review your six and put them in order using this question: which of these would I do at nine o’clock at night, on my own, feeling terrible, with no one watching?
Keep the top two or three and cross the rest out. A short list you use beats a long list you admire.
Check what is left
a.	It can be started in under five minutes, because on a bad day you will not start anything that cannot.
b.	It does not depend on anybody else being available at the time.
c.	It works in the actual place you will be, not in an imagined version of your life.
d.	You have done it at least once already and know that it does something for you.
You also need one step that prevents the pressure building up. Something regular and unremarkable, like a standing Wednesday walk, does more over a year than any emergency technique.
Write two or three steps for Inner peace, including one that is about stopping the pressure building up rather than dealing with it once it has.
5. Signs of success
Progress here is slow and mostly invisible, which makes it very easy to conclude that nothing is happening when quite a lot is.
Write from six months ahead
Imagine it is six months from now and this has gone reasonably well. Not perfectly, just reasonably. Describe an ordinary week from inside it.
What do your evenings look like in that week, hour by hour, from getting home to going to bed?
Something goes wrong on the Wednesday. What do you do with it, and how long does it take you to get past it?
What has stopped happening that used to happen every week without fail?
What would somebody who has not seen you for six months say when they saw you?
Write what you would notice. “I got to sleep before midnight most nights” can be checked against a real week, and “I felt calmer in myself” cannot.
6. Signs of concern
Stress shows up in three separate places, and you may only watch one of them. The one you notice last is usually the one that would have warned you earliest.
Check all three places

Write at least one warning sign under each of these three headings. If you cannot think of anything under one of them, ask somebody who knows you well, because they will have noticed something you have not.
In your body
Jaw, shoulders, stomach, sleep, appetite, headaches, that feeling in the chest. Where does it show up in you first?
In your thinking
Running the same argument over and over, everything feeling pointless, black and white thinking, or telling yourself that nobody would care anyway.
In what you do
Not answering the phone, cancelling things, drinking earlier in the day, being short with people, staying up later and later, or going quiet around other people.
What would be the first sign that Inner peace is slipping? Write something somebody could check.
7. Response to concern
You probably know what you ought to do when the pressure comes on, and at that moment it may all seem pointless. So write this box as advice to someone else.
Write to somebody else first
Picture a man, six months in, who has gone quiet. He is not sleeping, he has stopped going to things and he says there is no point ringing anybody because they have their own problems.
What would you say to him? Write it properly, in your own words.
What would you tell him to do first, tonight, before he does anything else?
He says he does not want to be a burden. What is your answer to that?
Now read back what you have written. How much of it applies to you, and what stops you taking your own advice?
Then make it a plan
If I notice __________, then within __________ I will __________.
The person I will tell is __________, and if I cannot reach them my second person is __________.
8. Progress, changes and support
Fill in the first part now, then come back to this box at every review.
Build on what you handled
You may have a poor record of what you have already handled, because the bad stretches are memorable and the ordinary coping is not.
Pick a difficult day in the last month that you got through without anything going wrong. What did you do that day?
Who or what helped, even a little, and did you tell them afterwards that it had?
What does that tell you about which of your steps is working?
Review questions
Has your rating changed, and if so, what changed it? If it went down, write that down, because it tells you where the plan needs work.
Which of your calming steps did you use, and which one turned out to be theoretical?
What support do you need that you are not getting, and have you asked for it yet?
Final check
Your steps include at least one thing that prevents pressure building, not only things that deal with it afterwards.
Every step could be started in five minutes on a bad night.
You have a warning sign in your body, one in your thinking, and one in what you do.
Your response includes a specific person and a backup person.
Nothing you have written could harm another person or put you at risk of offending. Checking Your Plan

blocks.x: This need is about hobbies, interests, fun, and being good at something. It covers what you do with the hours that are yours, and whether any of them give you something to look forward to. It takes in sport, music, fishing, cars, gardening, games, building things and anything else that you do because you want to rather than because you have to.

This need is not only about having fun, although fun is a perfectly good reason on its own. It also covers doing something you can get better at over time, because a particular kind of satisfaction comes only from being noticeably less bad at something than you were last year. Watching television or scrolling does not give you that feeling.

The other half of this need is balance. If your life is all work and obligation with nothing in it for you, you will eventually look for something, and you may not look sensibly. Adults are bad at this, because you may decide somewhere along the way that having interests is something for teenagers, and stop replacing the ones you lose.
Signs of progress
You have at least one thing in your week that you would be annoyed about having to cancel.
You are getting better at something, even slowly, and you could describe how.
Some of what you do involves other people, and some of it is just yours.
Your free time gets used on purpose rather than simply disappearing.
You could answer the question “what are you into” without having to think about it for a while.
Signs of drifting
Evenings and weekends run together into one long stretch with nothing in them you would remember afterwards.
The things you used to do have stopped, usually without any decision being made.
Boredom is a constant background hum rather than an occasional thing.
Your free time goes mostly to a screen, and you would rather not add up how much.
Somebody asks what you do for yourself and you cannot come up with anything.
If the second list fits you better than the first, give this section more time than it seems to need.
Why this need matters

Empty time is not a risk factor in itself, but other risk factors build on it. Think back to how things built up and look for long stretches of unstructured evening time, alone, with nothing much to do and nothing to look forward to. Boredom is more uncomfortable than it sounds, and an uncomfortable person will reach for whatever is closest and easiest. Building a week that has things in it is one of the most practical parts of the plan.
Eight boxes, and the prompts in this section are different again from the last two. Work through them in order.
1. Rate your ability
Rate it twice, because the comparison tells you more than either number does by itself.
Now, and back then
Rate Excellence in play as it is met today, 0 to 10.
Rate Excellence in play as it was met when you were about sixteen, 0 to 10.
What happened in between
If you score much lower now than you did then, ask what took the old hobbies away and whether any of those reasons still apply.
What does the gap between those two numbers tell you?
2. Why this matters to me
Not having the time can be a reason or an excuse. Before you write anything, read the two statements below.
Reasons and excuses
I would like to have more going on, but between work and everything else there is not much time for it at the moment.
I get home at half five and go to bed at eleven, which is five and a half hours, and at the moment almost none of it is spent on anything I would miss.

Both of those could be written by the same person on the same evening. The first one closes the subject down and the second one opens it up, because it has numbers in it that can be argued with. Write your answer in the second style.
How many hours of your own do you have in a normal week? Work it out roughly rather than guessing.
Where do those hours currently go? Be specific, because it is easy to round things down here.
What did you used to be into, and what did you like about it? Not the activity, the feeling underneath it.
What would you want to be able to say you were good at in three years?
3. This need and my offending
You may not think boredom caused your offending, and this box does not ask you to say it did. It asks what the empty time was doing, because it may have been the setting rather than the cause.
Write about your time, your boredom and what you were looking for. Do not describe the offending.
Sentence starters
In the year before things went wrong, the last thing I did purely because I enjoyed it was __________.
My evenings back then went like this: __________.
The hours where it happened were usually __________, and what I would otherwise have been doing at that time was __________.
It gave me something to do, and what it replaced was __________.
If I had had one thing in my week I looked forward to, what might have been different is __________.
Was your offending motivated by the Excellence in play need? Write what you wanted and how you felt at the time, not what you did.
4. Steps to meet this need
This box fails when you write down something ambitious that you never begin. The way through it is to plan for the obstacle instead of pretending it will not turn up.
Jog your memory
These are areas rather than answers, so use them to remember things you have not thought about in years. Do not write any of these words down as your step.

fishing / cards / guitar / bikes / running / bowls / darts / dogs / veggie garden / restoring something / woodwork / photography / cooking / chess / model building / swimming / walking group / choir / motorbikes / metal detecting / footy / volunteering / drawing / reading
Plan for obstacles
For each step you write, add the thing most likely to stop it and what you will do about that. A step written without its obstacle is a wish.
I will __________ on __________ at __________. The thing most likely to stop this is __________, and if that happens I will __________.
Check your answer
a.	At least one step costs nothing, because a plan that needs money will stall the first tight month.
b.	At least one step involves other people, since anything done entirely alone is very easy to drop.
c.	At least one step is something you could get better at over time rather than just pass time with.
d.	Every step has a day attached to it. Not a frequency, a day.

Pick things that are already running to a schedule somebody else sets, such as a club night or a class. Turning up to something that happens at seven on a Thursday whether you come or not is far easier than organising yourself from scratch every week.
Write two or three steps for Excellence in play, preferring things that already run to a schedule somebody else sets.
5. Signs of success
Success in this area shows up in your calendar before it shows up in how you feel, which makes it easier to check than most.
Describe the week
Describe what you would be doing in a good week six months from now.
Which nights of the week have something in them, and what?
What would somebody see if they looked in your shed, your kitchen or the boot of your car?
Who would you have spoken to that week who is not family and not from group?
What are you better at than you were six months ago, and how would you demonstrate it?
6. Signs of concern
Things rarely stop with a decision. They stop with a reason, and the reason sounds sensible at the time, so write it down in advance.
Write your excuses first
You probably have three or four standard lines you use when you are about to drop something. Write yours down now, while you are not using them.
What did you tell yourself last time you stopped going to something? Use the actual words.
How many weeks in a row would you have to miss before you had stopped going altogether?
What is the first thing to disappear from your week when you are not doing well?
Who would notice, and would they say anything?
Turn the answers into something checkable. “Two Thursdays missed in a row” is a warning sign you can act on. “Losing interest” tends to be recognised only long after it has happened.
7. Response to concern

The problem with restarting something you have dropped is that the full version feels like too much, so you may do nothing instead. The way around that is to decide now what the smallest possible version looks like.
Write the two-minute version
For each of your steps, work out the smallest version that still counts as doing it. Not the good version, the version you could not talk yourself out of.
Instead of __________, the smallest version is __________, which takes about __________ minutes.
If I have missed __________ in a row, then I will __________ before the next one comes around.
The person I will tell is __________, and what I will ask them to do is __________.

Walking to the end of the street counts as a walk. Ten minutes on the guitar counts as playing. The small version keeps the thing going, and a habit that is still going can be built back up, whereas one that has stopped has to be started again from the beginning.
What will you do when you notice that first warning sign for Excellence in play? Write one response for the first sign and a faster one if it keeps going.
8. Progress, changes and support
Fill in the first part now, and come back to this box at every review.
Sort what you have tried

By your first review you will have tried some things, and some of them will not have taken. Something that did not take is not a failure. You learn from it when you sort what you tried by what happened.
Which things did you keep doing, and what did they have in common?
Which ones fell over, and was it the activity itself, the timing, the cost, or the fact that you were doing it alone?
Which one would you put your money on for the next six months, and what would make it more likely to stick?
Review questions
How many nights in a typical week now have something in them? Compare that with the last review.
Is there anything you are now noticeably better at?
What support would help, and who could provide it?
Final check
Every step has an actual day attached to it, not a frequency.
At least one step costs nothing and at least one involves other people.
You have written the obstacle for each step and what you will do about it.
You have a two-minute version of each step for the weeks when the full version is beyond you.
Your steps could not harm another person or put you at risk of offending, and anything that involves children fits your legal conditions and your safety plan. Checking Your Plan

blocks.x: This need is about meaning and purpose, whatever those mean to you: whether your life adds up to something, and whether you could say what. For some people that is religion, and for others it is not, so the word is used here in a broader sense than usual.

Purpose in this sense is not grand. It rarely has anything to do with achievement or with leaving a mark on the world. Yours may be fairly plain: being a decent father, being the one who turns up when somebody needs a hand, keeping something going that would fall over without you, or looking after a bit of ground. How impressive it sounds does not count. What counts is whether it gives your ordinary weeks a meaning to you.

Do not skip this need, even if the word puts you off or the question feels as though it has no answer. A person who cannot say what their life is for is much easier to knock off course, because they have no way to measure a decision.
Signs of progress
You could say what matters to you and why, without having to make something up on the spot.
You have something in your life that you would keep doing even if nobody thanked you for it.
Your decisions mostly line up with what you say you believe, and where they do not, you notice.
Bad stretches are hard without being pointless, because they sit inside something larger.
You have some sense of the kind of man you are trying to be, separate from what you have done.
Signs of drifting
One week is much like the next and none of them seem to be heading anywhere in particular.
You could not say what you believe about much of anything, and you have not thought about it in years.
Things that used to matter to you have stopped mattering, and there was no moment where you decided that.
You find yourself thinking that none of it makes any difference either way.
What you do and what you say you believe have come apart, and you avoid looking at the gap.
Why this need matters

Two things make this need pressing after offending. The first is drift. Someone who has no sense of what his life is for has no way to weigh a decision. Decisions get made on whatever feels all right at the time, and small ones stack up in a direction nobody chose. The second is what happens afterwards. Offending tends to take away whatever sense of purpose a person had, and it can leave someone believing he is finished as a person and that nothing he does now counts. That belief is dangerous, because a man who thinks he has nothing left to protect has no reason to protect anything. Rebuilding a sense of purpose does not let you off. It gives you something to stay on course for.
Eight boxes. This section asks bigger questions than the last three, so give it more time and expect the answers to come out messier at first.
1. Rate your ability
Two scales here, not one, because they measure different things. Look at the distance between them.
Rate how important having a sense of purpose is to you, 0 to 10.
Rate how well that need is met in your life at the moment, 0 to 10.
Look at the gap

A large gap between those two numbers means you know this need matters and are not meeting it. A low score on both needs the same attention. It usually means one of two things: either this need is not important to you, or it has been unmet for so long that you have stopped expecting anything from it.
What does the gap between those two numbers tell you?
2. Why this matters to me
Approaching this head on rarely works, because “what is your purpose in life” is not a question anybody can answer cold. Come at it sideways instead.
Questions to think about
Pick two or three of these, and take longer over them than you would in other sections.
Think of somebody you respect, alive or dead, whom you have met in person. What is it about how they live that you respect?
What would you want a grandchild to know about you? Not what you would want hidden, what you would want known.
What is something you would still do even if nobody ever found out you had done it?
When did you last feel useful to somebody? What were you doing?
If you had to write down three things you believe are true about how people ought to treat each other, what would they be?
What do you want to be able to say you spent your fifties, sixties or seventies doing?

If nothing comes, write that rather than leaving the box empty, and raise it with your psychologist. “I have got nothing for this and it bothers me” is a complete answer and a better starting point than something invented to fill the space.
3. This need and my offending
The link here may be absence rather than pursuit. You may not say you offended in search of meaning, but you may recall a stretch beforehand where nothing seemed to matter much either way.
Write about what you believed, what you had stopped caring about and how you justified things to yourself. Do not describe the offending.
Sentence starters
In that period, what I would have said my life was for is __________.
The things that used to matter to me that had stopped mattering were __________.
The way I squared it with myself at the time was __________.
What I believed about myself back then was __________.
What I believe about myself now is __________, and the difference between those two is __________.
Was your offending motivated by the Spirituality need? Write what you wanted and how you felt at the time, not what you did.

Spend the longest on the third stem, the hardest one on the page. Anyone who has done something he knew was wrong had some way of justifying it at the time. Being able to describe your own version is a large part of making sure it cannot be used again.
4. Steps to meet this need
Purpose is built from things you do repeatedly, not decided in an afternoon, so the steps in this box look ordinary.
Areas for this need
Use these to jog your thinking rather than as answers.

being useful to someone / looking after something living / faith or a religious community / cultural connection / country and land / mentoring / repairing something broken / giving time / caring for a relative / keeping a family thing going / study / craft / conservation / being reliable / telling the truth consistently
Small repeated actions
A step here should be something that happens more than once, that costs you something, and that you would still do if nobody noticed.
Because I believe __________, I will __________ every __________.
Check your answer
a.	It describes something you do, not something you believe. Beliefs do not go in this box, actions do.
b.	It repeats. A one-off gesture does not build anything.
c.	It costs you something, whether that is time, effort or convenience, because things that cost nothing tend to mean nothing.
d.	You would still do it if nobody ever knew about it.

One caution for this section. Wanting to be useful to others is good. Where children are already part of your life, check every step against your legal conditions and your safety plan, and do not write a step that seeks out new contact with children. If something on your list is heading that way, stop and talk to your psychologist before you write it down, and leave that step off the list.
Write two or three steps for Spirituality. Each one needs a what, a when, and a where or a who.
5. Signs of success
Progress is hardest to see in this need, because it cannot be measured in the ordinary way. What you can look for is consistency between what you say and what you do.
Look for evidence
What in your week would somebody see as evidence of what you say matters to you?
When was the last time you did something inconvenient because it was the right thing to do? How often does that happen?
What have you kept going for more than three months without anybody making you?
If somebody asked you what you were about, could you answer without rehearsing it first?
6. Signs of concern
The warning signs here are mostly things you say to yourself rather than things you do, which makes them easy to miss. Write them down.
Thoughts you recognise
Read these and mark the ones you recognise. Then write the version you use, in your own words.
“None of this makes any difference anyway.”
“I am past it, there is no point starting anything now.”
“After what I have done, who am I to be talking about right and wrong.”
“Nobody would care either way.”

Look at the third one again. Feeling that you have forfeited the right to any values at all is a dangerous place to end up, because a man who believes he has nothing left to protect will not protect anything. Feeling ashamed of what you did and keeping to what you believe do not conflict, whatever it feels like.
7. Response to concern

Arguing yourself out of that kind of thinking on your own rarely works, because the thinking is very good at answering back. What works better is doing something small and concrete, and telling somebody.
Say it to somebody else
Picture a man saying, out loud, that after what he has done there is no point in him trying to be any particular kind of person.
What would you say back to him? Write it in your own words.
What would you suggest he do this week, rather than think?
Now read it back. How much of that applies to you, and what stops you accepting it?
Then make it a plan
If I catch myself thinking __________, then I will __________ and I will tell __________.
8. Progress, changes and support
Fill in the first part now, and expect this box to change more between reviews than any other in the workbook.
Start from evidence
Give one thing you have done in the last month that you would want known about you.
What made that possible, and could you do it more often?
Has anything you believe changed in the last year? What changed it?
Review questions
Are you doing what you said you would? Where has the gap opened up between what you believe and what you do?
Has your answer to “what is my life for” changed, and is the new one closer to true?
Who could help with this, and would you be willing to have that conversation?
Final check
Your steps are things you do rather than things you believe.
Each step repeats and each one costs you something.
Any step that involves children fits your legal conditions and your safety plan, and none of them seeks out new contact with children.
You have written down the actual words of the thinking that worries you, not a polite version of it.
Nothing you have written could harm another person or put you at risk of offending. Checking Your Plan

blocks.x: This need is about feeling good right now, in the moment, and enjoying something while it is happening. A decent feed, a hot shower after a cold day, sitting in the sun, laughing at something, the first ten minutes of a Saturday morning with nowhere to be.

It sounds like the least serious need on the list, and it is one of the most important. A life with no pleasure in it at all is not sustainable, and a person living one will eventually take pleasure from somewhere, sensibly or otherwise. Removing everything enjoyable from your life as a form of punishment is not a plan, it is a countdown.

Pleasures come in two kinds. Some are quick, intense and over in a moment, and they tend to leave you flatter than you were. Others are slower, milder and leave you better off afterwards. Both count, and a life built entirely from the first kind will keep needing a bigger dose.
Signs of progress
Most days have small things that you enjoy while they are happening.
You notice them at the time rather than only in hindsight.
Enjoying something does not come with a layer of guilt on top of it.
You can stay in an ordinary moment without needing it to be more than it is.
Most of what you enjoy is the slow kind rather than the quick kind.
Signs of drifting
Days go by in a flat grey with nothing in them either good or bad.
The only things that reliably do anything for you are quick, intense and over fast.
You feel you have no right to enjoy anything, so you do not let yourself.
You are mostly somewhere else in your head, either back in something that happened or ahead in something that might.
What used to be enough is no longer enough.
Why this need matters

This need connects to offending more directly than most, in two opposite ways. The first is that online offending is, among other things, a quick and reliable way of producing a strong feeling, and a flat life goes looking for that. The second is what happens afterwards. You may have left court determined that you no longer deserve to enjoy anything, and stripped your life back to work, sleep and obligation. That feels like taking it seriously, and for a few months it lasts. Then the emptiness becomes unbearable, and the plan has no answer for it, because enjoyment was ruled out at the start. Building ordinary pleasure back into your life does not let you off the hook. It stops the pressure building to the point where something has to give.
Eight boxes. This section asks you to admit something that can be uncomfortable to say: that you miss enjoying things.
1. Rate your ability
Rate yourself, then have a go at rating yourself as somebody else would. The two ratings may be further apart than you expect.
Rate Happiness as you see it today, 0 to 10.
Rate Happiness as somebody who knows you well would rate it, 0 to 10.
Why the numbers differ

A higher self-rating often means you are counting things you no longer do. A lower one often means you are being harder on yourself than the evidence supports. Either way, write a sentence about the gap.
What does the gap between those two numbers tell you?
2. Why this matters to me
This box may feel uncomfortable, because writing down that you want to enjoy your life can feel like asking for something you have forfeited. Write it anyway.
Questions to think about
What is the last thing you remember enjoying while it was happening rather than afterwards? How long ago was that?
What did you cut out of your life after everything happened, and was cutting it out necessary, or did it just feel appropriate?
What do you tell yourself when you catch yourself enjoying something?
If a mate said he had decided he was never going to enjoy anything again, what would you think of that plan?
What is something small and completely harmless that you would like to have back?
3. This need and my offending
Your answer here changes the plan more than almost any other box. Take your time.
Write about the feeling you were chasing, how long it lasted and what came after it. Do not describe the offending.
Sentence starters
What I was chasing was __________, and the closest ordinary thing to that feeling is __________.
It lasted about __________, and afterwards I felt __________.
Over time I needed __________ to get the same effect, which tells me __________.
Apart from this, the things in my life that gave me a lift were __________.
The pattern I can see now is __________.
Was your offending motivated by the Happiness need? Write what you wanted and how you felt at the time, not what you did.

Spend the longest on the third stem. Anything that needs to get bigger to keep working is a bad long-term arrangement, whatever it is, and seeing that pattern in yourself does more than any amount of resolve. See how one man answered this box
4. Steps to meet this need
The task here is to build a life with enough ordinary enjoyment in it that the flatness never gets bad enough to need rescuing.
List ten small things

Ten things you enjoy, or used to enjoy, that are completely harmless and cost little or nothing. Small is the point. If you are stuck, these are areas rather than answers: food, weather, water, music, animals, being outside, warmth, a task finished, quiet, company.
Sort them by speed
Review your ten and mark each one.
Fast
Strong, quick, over in minutes, and you often want another one straight after. Sugar, a drink, a big spend, anything on a screen designed to keep you there.
Slow
Milder, takes longer to arrive, lasts afterwards, and does not leave you wanting more. A long walk, cooking properly, being in water, a proper conversation, working on something with your hands.

You do not have to get rid of the fast ones, and a life with none of them in it would be joyless. Aim for balance. If nine of your ten are fast, your plan needs work in this box more than anywhere else.
Put three in your week
I will __________ on __________, which takes about __________ minutes.
a.	At least two of the three are the slow kind.
b.	Each one is small enough that a bad week would not stop it.
c.	None of it needs anybody else’s permission or availability.
d.	You would be comfortable with anybody knowing about all of it.
Write two or three steps for Happiness, and check each one against the test that you would be comfortable with anybody knowing about all of it.
5. Signs of success
The change here is subtle, and it is much easier to spot in what you are not doing than in what you are.
What would somebody else notice
Somebody who sees you weekly. What would look different about you, and would they be able to say why?
What would they hear you talk about that you do not talk about now?
What would have stopped, that they might notice before you do?
Six months from now, what would you have looked forward to that week?
One of the better signs in this area is a boring one: enjoying something without immediately following it with a reason why you should not have.
6. Signs of concern
Watch for two different warnings here. They look like opposites, so it is easy to watch for one and miss the other.
Trace back a flat stretch
Think of a period when everything went grey on you. Run it backwards and find the first sign.
Once it was clearly bad, what did your days look like?
Two weeks earlier, what had already gone? Usually something small drops off first.
What was the first thing you stopped bothering with?
Then check the other direction
The second warning is the opposite of flatness, and it is the more serious of the two.
Is anything in your life needing to get bigger, longer or more frequent to do what it used to do?
Is there anything you enjoy that you have started keeping to yourself?
If either of those last two questions produced an answer, do not sit on it. Raise it with your psychologist this week, or write the date you noticed it and review it at your next review.
7. Response to concern
Two warnings means two responses, and they are not the same response, so write both.
Build both as if-then
If everything has gone flat and I notice __________, then I will __________ within __________ and tell __________.
If I notice something needing to get bigger to work, or notice myself keeping something to myself, then I will tell __________ within __________.
The excuse I am most likely to use for not following through is __________, and my answer to it is __________.

The second response has to be faster and less negotiable than the first, and it needs to go to somebody who can do something about it. The secrecy is the danger there, more than whatever is being kept secret.
What will you do when you notice that first warning sign for Happiness? Write one response for the first sign and a faster, less negotiable one if it keeps going.
8. Progress, changes and support
Fill in the first part now, then come back at every review.
Build on what worked
Write down one moment in the last week that you enjoyed while it was happening. It can be tiny.
What made it possible, and how hard would it be to have that twice as often?
Did you let yourself enjoy it, or did you take something off it afterwards?
Review questions
Is the balance between fast and slow moving in the right direction?
Is there anything in your week now that you look forward to?
What support would help, and have you asked for it?
Final check
At least two of your three weekly steps are the slow kind.
You would be comfortable with anybody knowing about everything on your list.
You have written both warnings, the flatness one and the escalation one.
Your second response is faster and less negotiable than your first.
Nothing you have written could harm another person or put you at risk of offending. Checking Your Plan

blocks.x: This need is about feeling informed and understanding what is going on, so that you are not left in the dark, whether that is about your own case, your own health, a decision that affects you, or simply how something works. It does not require being clever, only having enough information that you are not left guessing.

This need is easy to underrate, because it does not announce itself the way hunger or loneliness do. It shows up sideways, as suspicion, as resentment, or as a flat refusal to ask a question you need answered because asking feels like admitting you do not already know. Left unmet for long enough, not knowing starts to feel like being deliberately kept out, whether or not that is true.

Feeling informed is not the same as having opinions about things, or as having taken in a great deal of information from any source that will provide it. It means understanding the things that affect your life, from people and sources you can check.
Signs of progress
When you do not understand something that affects you, you ask the person who knows, rather than guessing.
You know roughly where you stand on the things that matter, your obligations, your finances, your health, rather than avoiding looking at them.
You can tell the difference between something you have checked and something you have just heard.
Not knowing something makes you curious rather than defensive.
You are comfortable saying “I don’t know, I will find out” out loud.
Signs of drifting
You avoid asking questions because asking feels like exposing a gap.
You assume the worst about a situation because nobody has told you anything, and the silence fills with suspicion.
You have stopped opening letters, checking accounts, or asking about your own situation because not knowing feels safer than knowing.
You have strong opinions about things you have never checked.
You feel like everyone else is working from information you were never given.
If one line in those two lists described you, keep it in mind while you work through the boxes below.
Why this need matters

Feeling permanently kept in the dark, about your own case, your own supervision, your own family’s decisions, tends to push a person one of two ways, and neither helps. One is to stop asking altogether and disengage. The other is to go looking for answers in whatever source will give one, checked or not, private or not. Either way you end up running your life on guesswork and private theories instead of checked information, and a life like that is easier to justify to yourself in secret. Understanding your own situation, including your own patterns and your own risk, connects directly to Concept 18 of Understanding My Past, Understanding My Risk Factors. This need is where you put that understanding to use.
Eight boxes, same as every other section. Some ask what you already know, some ask what stops you finding out the rest.
1. Rate your ability
Do not guess this one from memory. Ask somebody a direct question first, then rate yourself against what they tell you.
Ask the person who knows

Pick one thing that affects you right now that you are not entirely sure about, a condition of your supervision, a fact about your case, a decision somebody else made about you. Ask the person who knows. Then answer these.
What did you think the answer was, before you asked?
What was the answer?
Rate this need overall
Rate Knowledge today, 0 to 10, where 0 means you are mostly guessing about the things that matter and 10 means you generally know where you stand and check what you do not.
If the gap between your guess and the actual answer was large, it usually means you have been avoiding the asking rather than lacking the ability to understand the answer.
2. Why this matters to me
Below is a bank of words for how it feels to be kept in the dark. Pick the two or three that fit you, then check your answer against the test underneath.
Suspicious. Small. Foolish. Excluded. Behind. Anxious. Resentful. Written off. Managed rather than told. Safer not knowing.
Check your words
a.	Have you described an actual situation, not just the general feeling?
b.	Have you said what you did in response, not just how you felt?
c.	Have you said whether the gap was because nobody told you or because you did not ask?
d.	Would somebody reading this know what specifically you want to understand better?
Why does Knowledge matter to you? Say what specifically you want to understand better, so somebody reading it would know.
3. This need and my offending
Your answer here changes the plan more than almost any other box. Take your time.
Write about what not knowing or not understanding felt like, and what it left you doing instead. Do not describe the offending.
Sentence starters
What I felt shut out of was __________, and I found out about it instead through __________.
Nobody explained __________ to me, so I decided for myself that __________.
The private theory I built instead of asking was __________.
If I had understood __________ at the time, I think I would have __________.
The pattern I can see now is __________.
Was your offending motivated by the Knowledge need? Write what you wanted and how you felt at the time, not what you did.

Spend the longest on the third stem, the private theory. Building a private theory instead of asking a question is a habit. Write the habit down, because a resolve to “communicate better” will not catch it next time. See how one man’s answer to this box went wrong
4. Steps to meet this need
The task is to build a habit of checking rather than guessing, in the specific places where you currently guess.
List what you are guessing
These can be about your case, your health, your finances, or a relationship. Anything you have an opinion about that you have not checked.
Turn each into a question
Not “find out more about my situation”. “Phone the service on Thursday and ask what the review process involves.”
Check your answer
a.	Each one is an actual question, not just a topic.
b.	Each one gives a specific person who can answer it.
c.	At least one of the three you could ask this week.
Write two or three steps for Knowledge, at least one of which you could ask about this week.
5. Signs of success
Find a time you already did this well, rather than starting from nothing.
Find the exception
Think of an occasion when you were confused or worried about something and went and asked, rather than guessing or avoiding it. Find one.
What was the situation, and what stopped you from just guessing that time?
Who did you ask, and how did you make yourself do it?
What would it take to do that more often, given you have clearly done it before?
6. Signs of concern
These are early, before the guessing has hardened into a fixed private theory.
Watch for these three
Are you avoiding opening something, a letter, an account, a message, because you would rather not know?
Have you caught yourself explaining somebody else’s decision to yourself, rather than asking them why they made it?
Is there a person you have stopped asking things, because you did not like a previous answer?

If you answered yes to any of those, do not wait until your next review. Raise it with your psychologist this week. If you cannot, write the date you noticed it and look at it again at your next review.
7. Response to concern
The response to this need is almost always the same: ask a specific person a specific question, sooner rather than later.
Build it as if-then
If I notice I am avoiding finding something out, then I will ask __________ within __________.
If I catch myself running a private theory about somebody else’s decision, then I will ask them directly within __________.
The excuse I am most likely to use for not asking is __________, and my answer to it is __________.
What will you do when you notice that first warning sign for Knowledge? Write down the excuse you are most likely to use for not asking, and your answer to it.
8. Progress, changes and support
Fill in the first part now, then come back at every review.
Build on what worked
Write down one thing you found out this month that you had previously been guessing about.
What made it possible to ask, and could you use the same approach again?
Review questions
Are you asking more, or still mostly guessing?
Is there a person you still avoid asking things?
What support would help, and have you asked for it?
Final check
Every box has something in it, even if what you have written is short.
Each of your steps gives a specific question and a specific person.
At least one of those steps is something you could start this week.
Your response to concern gives a person’s name, not “someone” or “my support network”.
Nothing you have written could harm another person or put you at risk of offending. Checking Your Plan

blocks.x: This need is about making things, expressing yourself and doing it your own way: having somewhere legitimate to put your own stamp on something, whether that is building, fixing, cooking, drawing, writing, music, growing things, or any other way of making rather than only consuming.

You may hear “creativity” and assume it does not apply to you because you do not paint or play an instrument. That reading is too narrow. The need is about making something that did not exist before and that has some part of you in it. It also covers having at least one part of your life where you set the terms instead of following somebody else’s.
Unmet, this need shows up as a flatness, a sense that every part of your day is either work or waiting, with nowhere that is yours.
Signs of progress
At least one thing in your week involves making or building something, rather than only consuming what somebody else made.
You have a way of doing at least one ordinary thing that is recognisably yours.
Finishing something you made gives you a specific kind of satisfaction that other things do not.
You are willing to be bad at something new for a while, because getting better at it counts for more than looking competent straight away.
Some part of your week is not dictated by anybody else’s rules.
Signs of drifting
Every hour of your week is either obligation or passive time, watching or scrolling rather than making.
You cannot remember the last time you finished making something.
You used to make things and stopped, and you have stopped noticing that you stopped.
Nothing in your life feels like it has your own stamp on it.
You avoid starting anything new because you do not want to be bad at it in front of anyone, including yourself.
If one line in those two lists described you, keep it in mind while you work through the boxes below.
Why this need matters

A life with no legitimate outlet for making or expressing anything tends to narrow to whatever is left. Check whether the narrowing happened around online behaviour that eventually became offending. The space was private, it was yours, and it was the one place you felt any control or mastery at all. This need is not a substitute explanation for offending, and it may not be true for you. Where it is true, rebuilding a legitimate space that is yours, where you make things and set your own terms, removes some of the pull that a private, ungoverned space once had.
Eight boxes, same as every other section. Some ask what you used to make, some ask what stops you making anything now.
1. Rate your ability
Rate where you are now, then work backwards through time until you find the point this dropped away, because that point usually tells you more than the current number does.
Rate today
Rate Creativity today, 0 to 10, where 0 means nothing in your life right now is something you make or shape yourself and 10 means it is a steady, regular part of your week.
Now trace it backwards
Go back year by year, or in whatever chunks make sense for you, until you reach a point where this need was clearly better met than it is now. Stop there.
When was Creativity last properly met, roughly, and what were you making or shaping then?
What changed around then that took it away?

The cause may be something ordinary, moving house, a busy stretch at work, money, rather than a decision to stop. Ordinary causes are good news, because they mean the cause is not something permanent about you.
2. Why this matters to me
Come at it from a few angles. Pick the two or three that bring something to mind.
Questions to think about
What is something you have made, in any sense of the word, that you were proud of, even if you never told anyone?
Is there a version of yourself, a hobby, a skill, a way of doing things, that you have lost touch with and miss more than you let on?
What do you do at the moment where you set your own rules, rather than following somebody else’s?
If someone took away every screen in your house for a month, what would you do with your hands?
3. This need and my offending
Your answer here changes the plan more than almost any other box. Take your time.
Write about what the behaviour gave you that felt like it was yours, private, or under your own control, and how that felt. Do not describe the offending.
Sentence starters
What felt like mine, private and under my own control, was __________.
Nowhere else in my life at the time did I feel that same sense of __________.
If I had a legitimate version of that feeling somewhere else, it might have looked like __________.
The pattern I can see now is __________.
Was your offending motivated by the Creativity need? Write what you wanted and how you felt at the time, not what you did.

Spend the longest on the last stem. A private, ungoverned space fills a need. Write down the need underneath it, because resolving to avoid the space leaves the need where it was. See how one man’s answer to this box went wrong
4. Steps to meet this need
The task is to build something of your own back into your week, on a scale small enough that it will happen.
Pick one thing to make
It does not have to be new. Returning to something you used to do counts, and is often easier than starting from nothing.
Make it small enough
Not “get back into woodworking”. “Fix the loose shelf bracket this Saturday morning using the tools I already have.”
Check your answer
a.	It points to an actual thing, not a category.
b.	It has a day and a place attached.
c.	It does not depend on buying something you cannot currently afford.
Write two or three steps for Creativity, none of which depend on buying something you cannot currently afford.
5. Signs of success
Progress here shows up in what you have made, which is easier to check than a feeling.
What would somebody else notice
Somebody who sees your house or your week regularly. What would they notice you had made or started?
What would you be able to show somebody, that you cannot show them now?
What would you talk about that you do not currently talk about?
6. Signs of concern
These are early, before the flatness has fully set back in.
Trace back a flat stretch
Think of a period when you made nothing and everything felt like obligation or passive time. Run it backwards and find the first sign.
Once it was clearly flat, what did your evenings look like?
What was the first thing you stopped bothering with?
If you found a first sign, do not wait until your next review. Raise it with your psychologist this week. If you cannot, write the date you noticed it and look at it again at your next review.
7. Response to concern
Two different situations call for two different responses here, so write both.
Build both as if-then
If a fortnight goes by and I have made nothing, then I will __________ and tell __________.
If I notice I am spending time somewhere private that I would not want anybody to see, then I will tell __________ within __________.
The excuse I am most likely to use for not following through is __________, and my answer to it is __________.
What will you do when you notice that first warning sign for Creativity? Write down the excuse you are most likely to use, and your answer to it.
8. Progress, changes and support
Fill in the first part now, then come back at every review.
Build on what worked
Write down one thing you made or finished in the last month, however small.
What made it possible, and could you use the same approach again?
Review questions
Is there more of your week that is fully yours than there was last time?
What support would help, and have you asked for it?
Final check
Every box has something in it, even if what you have written is short.
Each of your steps gives an actual thing, with a day and a place attached.
At least one of those steps is something you could start this week.
Your response to concern gives a person’s name, not “someone” or “my support network”.
