blocks.x: This need is about belonging to something bigger than yourself: a place, a group, or a role where you belong, rather than one where you are merely tolerated or present. Close relationships get their own section later, and this need is about a wider sense of fitting somewhere.

Belonging is not the same as being around people. A man can be surrounded by people all day at work and still have nowhere he belongs, and a man who lives alone can belong solidly to a club, a church, a team, or a street. The question is whether there is a “we” anywhere in your life that you are part of, not just present for.

This need is easy to let go, because losing it rarely feels like a single event. Usually it is a slow drift: missing a few things, feeling slightly more like a visitor each time, until you have stopped going altogether and barely noticed the last time you did.
Signs of progress
You have at least one group, place, or activity where people would notice if you stopped turning up.
You feel like a participant somewhere, not just a visitor or a name on a list.
You could ask somebody in that group for a favour without it feeling strange.
At least one group of people has some idea what is going on in your life.
Being part of something does not depend entirely on one other person.
Signs of drifting
You cannot name a single group or place where somebody would notice your absence.
You have stopped going to things you used to be part of, and nobody has chased you about it.
Whenever you are in a group, you feel like you are watching it rather than in it.
All of your sense of belonging runs through one single relationship, so if that person is unavailable, you have nowhere.
You assume any group would rather you were not there, without having tested that assumption recently.
If one line in those two lists described you, keep it in mind while you work through the boxes below.
Why this need matters

Isolation from any ordinary, positive group can be part of the pattern behind offending. Being alone does not cause it directly. A person with nowhere he belongs has nobody around him who would notice a slide, and nowhere that pulls him back toward an ordinary life when things get hard. Rebuilding some form of belonging, a group, a role, a regular place, puts ordinary people back in a position to notice, and gives you somewhere to be pulled back towards.
Eight boxes, same as every other section. Some ask where you already belong, some ask where you have stopped trying.
1. Rate your ability
Rate yourself, then rate yourself as somebody who has known you a long time would rate you. This need is often judged differently from the outside than from within.
Rate Community as you see it today, 0 to 10.
Rate Community as somebody who has known you a long time would rate your sense of belonging, 0 to 10.
Why the numbers differ

A lower self-rating than the other person’s guess often means you feel like an outsider somewhere that would count you in. A higher one often means you are counting a group you have already drifted away from. Either way, write a sentence about the gap.
What does the gap between those two numbers tell you?
2. Why this matters to me
Come at it from a few angles. Pick the two or three that bring something to mind.
Questions to think about
Where in your life, at any point, did you feel like you properly belonged rather than just attended?
What would you miss most about not being part of any group at all, if it turned out to be permanent?
Is there somewhere you already half-belong, that you could go back to instead of starting somewhere new?
Who would notice if you stopped showing up somewhere, right now?
3. This need and my offending
Your answer here changes the plan more than almost any other box. Take your time.
Write about the sense of belonging or connection you were chasing, and what being isolated from ordinary groups had left you without. Do not describe the offending.
Sentence starters
The sense of belonging I did not have anywhere else was __________.
By the time this became a problem, the ordinary groups I had drifted away from were __________.
If I had felt like I belonged somewhere ordinary at the time, I think __________.
The pattern I can see now is __________.
Was your offending motivated by the Community need? Write what you wanted and how you felt at the time, not what you did.

Spend the longest on the last stem. Isolation from ordinary groups rarely happens on its own. It usually clears the way for something else to fill the gap, so write what it made room for. A resolve to “get out more” is not enough. See how one man’s answer to this box went wrong
4. Steps to meet this need
The task is to find or rebuild one place you belong, on a scale small enough that it will happen.
Pick a group or activity
It can be something you used to belong to, something new, or something you already half-belong to and have let slide.
Write the smallest first move
Not “get more involved in the community”. “Turn up to Tuesday training and stay for the after-session coffee instead of leaving straight away.”
Check your answer
a.	It points to an actual place or group, not a category.
b.	It has a day attached.
c.	It does not depend on someone else inviting you first.
Write two or three steps for Community, none of which depend on someone else inviting you first.
5. Signs of success
Progress here is easier to see from outside than from inside, so borrow an outside view.
Ask it from outside yourself
If somebody from that group described you in six months, what would they say about how involved you are?
What would they say you had contributed, however small?
Would they say your absence would be noticed now, where it might not have been before?
6. Signs of concern
These are early, before the drift away from a group has become a lasting absence.
Trace back a drift
Think of a group or activity you used to be part of and are not any more. Run it backwards and find the first sign.
Once you had clearly stopped going, what had your attendance looked like in the weeks before that?
What was the first excuse you used to miss one session, that then became easier to use again?
If you found a first excuse, do not wait until your next review. Raise it with your psychologist this week. If you cannot, write the date you noticed it and look at it again at your next review.
7. Response to concern
Two different situations call for two different responses here, so write both.
Build both as if-then
If I notice I have missed two sessions or gatherings in a row, then I will __________ before the third.
If I notice I feel like an outsider somewhere I am supposed to belong, then I will tell __________ within __________.
The excuse I am most likely to use for not going back is __________, and my answer to it is __________.
What will you do when you notice that first warning sign for Community? Write down the excuse you are most likely to use for not going back, and your answer to it.
8. Progress, changes and support
Fill in the first part now, then come back at every review.
Build on what worked
Write down one moment in the last month when you felt you belonged somewhere, even briefly.
What made that possible, and could you get more of it?
Review questions
Is there more of a “we” in your life now than there was last time?
What support would help, and have you asked for it?
Final check
Every box has something in it, even if what you have written is short.
Each of your steps gives an actual place or group, with a day attached.
At least one of those steps is something you could start this week.
Your response to concern gives a person’s name, not “someone” or “my support network”.
Nothing you have written could harm another person or put you at risk of offending. Checking Your Plan

blocks.x: This need is about having a say in your own life and making your own decisions, from the ordinary ones up: what you eat, how you spend an evening, what you spend money on. Without it, everything feels decided for you or around you.

You may be constrained in some of this need right now, by supervision conditions, reporting obligations, or decisions other people have had to make. Those constraints are real, and this section is not a place to work out how to get around them. It covers the space that is left once they are accounted for, and how much of that space you use.

Feeling that you have no say anywhere in your life wears you down over time, whatever the reason. Pushing against the constraints that are there does not fix that. Notice and use the choices that still exist, because there are usually more of them than a powerless feeling lets you see.
Signs of progress
You make decisions, even small ones, instead of drifting along with whatever happens.
You know the difference between a constraint that exists and one you have assumed without checking.
You can say what you think, to the people it is appropriate to say it to, without it feeling dangerous.
You have at least a few areas of your life where the decision is up to you.
Having a condition or an obligation does not feel the same as having no life of your own at all.
Signs of drifting
You feel like everything in your life is decided by somebody else, all the time, in every area.
You have stopped making even the small decisions that are up to you.
You assume a restriction applies more broadly than it does, and have never checked.
You feel resentful most of the time, without necessarily being able to say at what, specifically.
You have started testing rules in small ways nobody sees, as a way of feeling like you still have some control.
If one line in those two lists described you, keep it in mind while you work through the boxes below.
Why this need matters

A man who feels he has no legitimate say anywhere in his life is at risk of taking back a sense of control somewhere illegitimate. Examples are testing a rule, keeping a small secret, or doing something because nobody said he could not. The pattern comes from the powerless feeling, not from the rule. Pushing back against lawful constraints does not fix it. Finding and using the ordinary choices that remain does, because then the feeling of having no say stops being accurate.
Eight boxes, same as every other section. Some ask where you already have choices, some ask where you have stopped noticing them.
1. Rate your ability
Rate how much say you feel you have, then count how many decisions you made this week without simply going along with somebody else. The two numbers do not always match.
Rate how much say you feel you have in your own life, 0 to 10.
Count your decisions
Think back over the last seven days. Count the decisions, however small, where you chose instead of defaulting.
How many decisions did you make this week? Write the number.
If the feeling and the count do not match, why?
A low feeling with a reasonable count can mean you are not giving yourself credit for the choices you make. If the feeling is high and the count is low, look closer.
2. Why this matters to me
Imagine a mate in a similar position to yours came to you for advice about feeling like he had no say in anything. Answer as if you were talking to him, then notice how it applies to you.
Advice to somebody else
What would you tell him he still has a say over, even with restrictions in place?
What would you tell him to stop assuming he cannot do, without checking?
What would you warn him against, if he started trying to claw back control in the wrong places?
3. This need and my offending
Your answer here changes the plan more than almost any other box. Take your time.
Write about the feeling of control or defiance the behaviour gave you, and what feeling powerless elsewhere had left unaddressed. Do not describe the offending.
Sentence starters
The feeling of having no say that I was carrying at the time was about __________.
What the behaviour gave me that felt like control was __________.
If I had felt like I had a say somewhere legitimate, I think __________.
The pattern I can see now is __________.
Was your offending motivated by the Independence need? Write what you wanted and how you felt at the time, not what you did.

Spend the longest on the last stem. A feeling of powerlessness looking for somewhere to reassert itself is a pattern, and it will have shown up more than once. Write where it showed up, because a general resolve to “take back control” does not say where. See how one man’s answer to this box went wrong
4. Steps to meet this need
The task is to find a legitimate choice and use it, not to push against a restriction.
Pick an area you control
Something small and completely within bounds, what you cook, how you spend a free evening, what you spend your own money on.
Make a decision this week
Not “have more control over my life”. “Choose and cook a proper meal on Wednesday instead of whatever is easiest.”
Check your answer
a.	It falls in a legitimate area, not something restricted.
b.	It has a day attached.
c.	You choose it, rather than somebody else doing it for you.
Write two or three steps for Independence. Each one is something you choose for yourself.
5. Signs of success
Progress here looks like fewer decisions given up by default, which you can check.
What would somebody else notice
Somebody who spends time with you regularly. What would they notice about how often you make a choice instead of going along with things?
What would you say out loud now that you would have kept to yourself before?
What would have stopped feeling like something being done to you, and started feeling like something you chose?
6. Signs of concern
This box has two warnings. They look like opposites, so it is easy to watch for one and miss the other.
Check both directions
Have you stopped making even the small decisions that are up to you, and just gone along with whatever happens instead?
Have you started testing a rule or a boundary in a small way, to see what you can get away with?
If either of those is true for you, do not leave it until your next review. Raise it with your psychologist this week, or write the date you noticed it and review it then.
7. Response to concern
Each warning needs its own response, so write both.
Build both as if-then
If I notice I have stopped making even small decisions for myself, then I will __________ within __________.
If I notice I am testing a rule or boundary in a small way, then I will tell __________ within __________.
The excuse I am most likely to use for not following through is __________, and my answer to it is __________.
What will you do when you notice that first warning sign for Independence? Write the excuse you are most likely to use, and your answer to it.
8. Progress, changes and support
Fill in the first part now, then come back at every review.
Build on what worked
Write one decision you made in the last month that was up to you.
What made that possible, and could you get more of it?
Review questions
Is your count of decisions this week higher than it was last time?
What support would help, and have you asked for it?
Final check
Every box has something in it, even if what you have written is short.
Each of your steps is in a legitimate area, not a restricted one.
At least one of those steps is something you could start this week.
Your response to concern gives a person’s name, not “someone” or “my support network”.
Nothing you have written could harm another person or put you at risk of offending. Checking Your Plan

blocks.x: This need is about being good at what you do, mastering something, and getting better at it over time. It does not have to be paid employment. Volunteering, study, running a household properly, or a serious hobby can all meet it, though paid work may supply much of it for you.

Mastery gives you a version of yourself that is good at something specific and checkable, instead of a vague sense of being adequate or not. It also provides one of the steadiest sources of daily structure a life can have, and unstructured time is where other problems tend to grow.

This need can go unmet in two ways that look similar from the outside. One is having no work or role at all. The other is having one but never getting better at it, going through the motions without building skill or pride.
Signs of progress
You have a role, paid or not, that gives structure to an ordinary day or week.
You have something specific you are good at, that you could point to.
You are still getting better at something, rather than having stopped improving years ago.
Doing the work itself gives you something, not only the outcome or the pay at the end of it.
You would be comfortable describing what you do to somebody who asked.
Signs of drifting
Your days have no structure, and one blends into the next.
You cannot think of anything you are good at, only things you get by on.
You have not improved at anything in longer than you can comfortably say.
Work, if you have it, is something you endure rather than something you get anything from.
You avoid describing what you do, because you do not think much of it yourself.
If one line in those two lists described you, keep it in mind while you work through the boxes below.
Why this need matters

Unstructured time and a flat sense of being no good at anything in particular are both well-established factors in offending. Idleness does not cause harm directly. An unstructured day leaves far more room for private, ungoverned time, and a low sense of competence anywhere legitimate can make a private source of mastery or control, however unhealthy, feel more important than it should. Rebuilding structure and a checkable sense of being good at something reduces both pressures.
Eight boxes, same as every other section. Some ask what you are good at, some ask what has stopped you using it.
1. Rate your ability
Rate how competent you feel at something, then rate how much you use that competence day to day. Having a skill and using it are not the same thing.
Rate how competent you feel at the thing you are best at, 0 to 10.
Rate how much of your week involves using that skill, 0 to 10.
Why the numbers differ
A skill you rate highly but rarely use is sitting idle for a reason, and the reason tells you more than the skill does.
If you rate a skill highly but rarely use it, write it here, with what keeps it out of your week.
2. Why this matters to me
Below is a bank of words people use for how it feels to have no structure or sense of mastery. Pick the two or three that fit, then check your answer against the test underneath.
Adrift. Adequate at best. Wasted. Restless. Bored. Purposeless. Going through the motions. Behind where I should be. Unused.
Check your words
a.	Have you written a specific role, task or skill, not just the general feeling?
b.	Have you said what a normal day currently looks like, structured or not?
c.	Have you said whether the gap is about having no role, or having one you are not improving at?
d.	Would somebody reading this know what specifically you want more competence or structure in?
Why does Work matter to you? Say what specifically you want more competence in, so somebody reading it would know.
3. This need and my offending
Your answer here changes the plan more than almost any other box. Take your time.
Write about the sense of competence, mastery or structure the behaviour gave you, and what an unstructured or purposeless stretch of time had left open. Do not describe the offending.

What the behaviour gave me that felt like skill or mastery was __________.

The pattern I can see now is __________.
Was your offending motivated by the Work need? Write what you wanted and how you felt at the time, not what you did.

Spend the longest on the last stem. Unstructured time and an absent sense of mastery tend to travel together, so write both down. A general resolve to “get busier” does not tell you what to change. See how one man’s answer to this box went wrong
4. Steps to meet this need
The task is to build structure and growing competence.
Pick one thing to improve
Paid work, a trade skill, study, or running your household properly all count.
Attach a repeated action
Not “get better at my job”. “Ask my supervisor on Monday to show me the part of the job I have never been trained on.”
Check your answer
a.	It points to an actual skill or role, not a category.
b.	It has a day and an action attached.
c.	It is something you would notice yourself doing differently in a week.
Write two or three steps for Work, each one something you would notice yourself doing differently in a week.
5. Signs of success
Progress here shows up as structure and competence you can point to, which is easier to check than a feeling.
What would somebody else notice
Somebody who works with you or sees your week. What would they notice about your days having more structure?
What would you be able to do now that you could not do six months ago?
What would they say if asked whether you are good at what you do?
6. Signs of concern
These are early, before unstructured time has become the norm again.
Trace back an unstructured stretch
Think of a period when your days had little shape and you were not building anything. Run it backwards and find the first sign.
Once your days had clearly lost their structure, what did a typical one look like?
What was the first routine or task you stopped doing?
If you can say what that first dropped routine was, do not leave it until your next review. Raise it with your psychologist this week, or write the date you noticed it and review it then.

What will you do when you notice that first warning sign for Work? Write the excuse you are most likely to use, and your answer to it.

Build on what worked
Write one thing you got better at, however small, in the last month.
What made that possible, and could you use the same approach again?
Review questions

What support would help, and have you asked for it?
Final check

blocks.x: This need is about closeness with the people who matter to you: having at least one adult relationship in your life with closeness in it, somebody you can be honest with and who knows something true about how you are, as well as how you present.

This section is about adult relationships only: a partner, family members, friends. It is not the place to work through anything to do with contact with children, including your own. Any question about contact with a child is governed by legal orders, case workers, and the professionals involved in that specific decision, not by this workbook, and this section does not touch it. If that is unresolved for you, take it to your caseworker or your psychologist, or to Legal Aid or a family lawyer in your state or territory. Do not work it out alone.

Closeness is not the same as having people around. You may have family nearby, or a partner in the house, and still have nobody who knows what is going on with you. This need is met by depth in at least one relationship.
Signs of progress
At least one adult knows something true and current about how you are, not a version you have edited for them.
You can be disagreed with by somebody close to you without the relationship feeling at risk.
You ask how somebody else is doing and wait for the answer.
You would tell at least one person if things were going badly, rather than managing it alone.
Closeness with someone does not depend entirely on them not knowing something important about you.
Signs of drifting
Everybody in your life gets a managed, edited version of you, and nobody gets the rest.
You cannot think of anybody you would tell if things were going badly.
Conversations with people close to you stay on the surface, weather, logistics, nothing underneath.
You assume that if people knew you, they would not want to be close to you.
Being around people and being close to somebody have started to feel like the same thing, so you have stopped noticing the difference.
If one line in those two lists described you, keep it in mind while you work through the boxes below.
Why this need matters

Isolation from adult closeness is one of the better-established patterns behind offending, and it has two effects. It removes the people most likely to notice a slide early, and it can leave a private, unmet need for closeness looking for somewhere else to be met, sometimes somewhere it should never have gone. Rebuilding closeness with an adult who knows the true version of you gives you a legitimate place to meet this need and puts somebody in a position to notice if things start to go wrong.
Eight boxes, same as every other section. Some ask who already knows the true version of you, some ask what stops you letting them.
1. Rate your ability
Rate yourself, then have a go at rating yourself as the person closest to you would. You may be surprised by the gap.
Rate Relationships as you see it today, 0 to 10.
Rate how close you are as the adult closest to you would rate it, 0 to 10.
Why the numbers differ

A higher self-rating than theirs usually means you are counting proximity as closeness. A lower one usually means you do not give the relationship credit for what it provides. Either way, write a sentence about the gap.
What does the gap between those two numbers tell you?
2. Why this matters to me
Look at it from a few angles. Pick the two or three you have most to say about.
Questions to think about
Who, if anyone, currently knows something true and current about how you are?
What is the cost, over time, of the edited version of you that other people get?
Is there a relationship in your life that has room for more honesty than it has now, if you let it?
What would it mean to you to be known by one other adult, instead of managed by everyone?
3. This need and my offending
Your answer here changes the plan more than almost any other box. Take your time.
Write about the closeness or connection you were missing in your adult relationships, and what that absence felt like. Do not describe the offending.
Sentence starters
The closeness I was missing in my adult relationships at the time was __________.
The person I could have gone to instead, but did not, was __________, and the reason I did not was __________.
If I had let one adult see the true version of me at the time, I think __________.
The pattern I can see now is __________.

The task is to bring more honesty into one existing adult relationship.

blocks.x: The introduction set out four ways a plan goes wrong: a harmful route, a plan that is too narrow, goals that fight each other, and steps you do not yet have enough to work with. Use this page to find them in your own plan. It only works once you have something written in every one of the eleven need sections, so come back to this page after Relationships rather than partway through.
Reading all box 4 answers

Before you check for any particular fault, open every need section and read only the box 4 answers, the steps, one after another, without stopping to read anything else. Reading eleven steps side by side shows up things you cannot see when you read them one section at a time, weeks apart.
Fault one: harmful route
A step can meet a need and still be the wrong step, either because it puts you somewhere you have no business being or because meeting the need this way would hurt somebody else.
Does any step involve children in a way your legal conditions or your safety plan do not allow, or seek out new contact with children, such as supervising, coaching or minding?
Does any step depend on nobody else knowing what you are doing?
Would you be comfortable reading every one of your eleven sets of steps aloud to your psychologist, or to the person you chose in “sharing your plan”?
Does any step rely on you being alone with somebody who could not consent to what you are asking of them, or on a situation you have engineered rather than one that arose naturally?
Fault two: too narrow
A plan that depends heavily on two or three needs and leaves the rest nearly empty holds up until something knocks out one of those two or three, and then the plan has no other support.
Which need sections have little or nothing written in box 4? Go and look, rather than guessing from memory.
If you imagine losing your two strongest needs tomorrow, a job ending or a relationship breaking down, is there anything left in the other nine that would hold you up?
Are three or more of your eleven steps the same step written out slightly differently, for example “spend more time with family” appearing under three different needs?
Fault three: conflicting goals
Two goals can both be good and still be impossible to have at once. If you have not decided in advance which one gives way, life will decide for you, usually at the worst moment.
List all eleven of your box 4 steps in one place. Do any two of them need the same hours of the same day?
Does meeting one need on your list undercut another, for example a work step that leaves no time or energy for the relationships or play steps?
If two steps did collide in a given week, have you decided which one wins, or would you be deciding that for the first time under pressure?
Fault four: missing resources
A step can be a good step and still fail because it needs a skill, some money, transport, a licence or an opportunity that you do not currently have.
Does any step depend on money you do not currently have spare?
Does any step depend on a skill, a licence or a piece of equipment you do not yet have, with no earlier step written in to get it?
Does any step depend on somebody else’s permission or availability, with no plan for what happens if they say no or are not around?
A gap like this does not make a goal a bad one. The goal is missing its own first step, so add that step instead of dropping the goal.
If this check changes something

Go back into the relevant need section and change the box 4 answer directly. You do not need to explain the change anywhere, and finding a fault here does not mean you failed the workbook. It means the check worked.
Removing a step from the page is not the same as removing whatever caused it.

A handful of words in this workbook come from research or from the SafeCare model rather than everyday English. Here is what each one means. Tapping a linked word anywhere in the workbook brings you straight to its entry here, and each entry has a link back to where you were.
What each word means here
Fundamental needs

The handful of basic, ordinary things every person is chasing: feeling well, feeling calm, feeling close to somebody, feeling like they are good at something, and feeling like their life adds up to something. Nobody has to be taught to want any of these, and wanting them was never the problem. This workbook works through eleven of them, one section each. A Good Lives Model term.
Pseudo Adult
One of three parts of a person described in the SafeCare model. The grown-up front you learned to put on, the face the world sees. See also Inner Child and True Adult.
Inner Child

One of three parts of a person described in the SafeCare model. The part of you that got stuck at the age when something happened that you could not handle. It does not go anywhere and is not meant to. It is not a stage you get past or something to be got rid of. See also Pseudo Adult and True Adult.
True Adult

One of three parts of a person described in the SafeCare model. The grown-up child, made up of all three parts, and its job is to act as the umpire between the other two. An umpire needs two sides on the field. The True Adult listens to the Pseudo Adult, listens to the Inner Child, and decides. It does not silence either of them, and it never stops having the job.
Approach goals

Things you are going to do, rather than only things you are going to stop doing. A plan made only of rules about what to avoid is not yet a life, so this workbook asks for approach goals throughout. A Good Lives Model term.

blocks.x: Purpose

This guide sets out how to run or support Planning My Future, the eleven-need workbook this library is built around. The register is professional, written for a facilitator, but nothing in it is restricted from anyone who reads it. If you are the person working through the plan rather than running it for somebody else, most of this will read as background rather than instruction, and that is fine. Read the sections on the safety boundary and on the four faults either way.

This guide assumes you have already read How to Use This Workbook, which explains the eight-box structure directly to the person working through it. This document does not repeat that explanation. It covers what a facilitator needs to do around it.
How the workbook is built

Eleven fundamental needs, each with the same eight-box structure, in a fixed order that runs from more concrete needs to ones that take more thinking. Life opens the sequence and Relationships closes it deliberately, because the closer needs benefit from everything the person has already worked through. Each need’s example page dissects weak answers rather than supplying a model to copy, following the library’s example-page pattern, so do not treat an example page as a template.
Box 3 in every section, “This need and my offending”, changes the plan more than almost any other box. It is also the one box with a hard safety boundary built into it.
Box 3 safety boundary

Every box 3 asks for feeling and motivation, never method. The instruction on the page already tells the group member this and tells them to stop and raise it with you if their answer starts heading into method. Your job is to be that person.

blocks.head: Redirecting a box 3 answer
blocks.x: Stop the writing there. Do not let the account continue to a natural end out of politeness. Acknowledge the feeling part of what they wrote, since that part was the task and is often the hardest part to say out loud. Then explain plainly that the written plan may be read by others and that describing method in it is not what any box in this workbook asks for. What comes next is a conversation with you, not more writing. Checking Your Plan uses the same escalation wording for the harmful-route fault. Use that wording instead of improvising your own in the moment, so group members hear one consistent message across the workbook and not a different version from each facilitator.

Expect this to come up, and plan for it before the first session where box 3 is reached. Know in advance who a group member is referred to if the conversation brings up something beyond what this workbook or this group is set up to deal with.
Pacing a group through it
This workbook has no session-by-session mapping, unlike the SafeCare concept series, so treat the following as a starting structure, not a fixed curriculum.
Open with the introduction and how-to-use sections in a single session, since both are short and the workbook does not make sense without them.

One need per session is a reasonable default pace. Shorter or more straightforward needs can be paired in a single session if the pace is going well; do not pair two needs if either produced a difficult box 3 disclosure in earlier work.
Build in time in each session for box 3 specifically, because sessions run long there and should be allowed to.

Individualise every plan. The prompts, word banks and sentence stems are a scaffold, not a script. An answer that closely matches somebody else’s or an example page is a sign to slow down, not a sign of a session going well.
Supporting faults and review

Once a person has something in box 4 for every need, the four faults check tests the plan as a set for a harmful route, being too narrow, goals that fight each other, or not enough to work with. The first time, walk through it together instead of leaving it as a solo exercise, since a harmful route in a person’s own plan is easier to miss from the inside.

The review process, and the shorter My Review tool built for repeated solo use afterward, both depend on the person having somebody to share the plan with. Help them choose that person deliberately during the sharing section instead of letting it default to whoever is nearest, and follow up on whether the conversation with that person took place.
Low literacy or no facilitator

For lower reading levels, read sections aloud, allow spoken answers to be written down by whoever is supporting, and use the worked examples to show the level of specificity being asked for, not the content. Short, honest answers are the standard everywhere in this workbook; do not let shorter answers read as the workbook not working for him.

The workbook itself is written to work with nobody present at all, years after any group has ended. If you are supporting somebody using it that way rather than running a group, everything above about box 3 and the four faults still applies. It simply means you are the one person they have, rather than one of several.
Scope note: fidelity monitoring

This guide does not include a GLM fidelity monitoring tool or a session-by-session fidelity checklist. For that material, use Prescott, Willis and Ward’s GLM Fidelity Monitoring Tool. Do not read this guide as a fidelity instrument.
Cautions
This workbook is not a risk assessment and does not replace one. Continue to use whatever validated tool and structured professional judgement process your service already applies.

Be clear with the people you support at the outset about the limits of confidentiality and any mandatory reporting duties that apply in your jurisdiction, in the same terms the introduction already sets out to them directly.

The approach-goal model this workbook uses is based on evidence that traditional, avoidance-only relapse prevention worksheets do not reduce reoffending (see References). That evidence is about worksheet design. It does not mean any particular person’s risk is low, so do not let this workbook’s tone soften how you communicate risk elsewhere.
Purpose

This brief sets out the approach for the relapse prevention component: two plans, one for online child exploitation material offending and one for contact offending. Two further components sit alongside either plan, on reporting obligations and on prepared disclosure. The register is professional, written for a facilitator, but nothing in it is restricted from a reader. If you are the person completing a plan rather than running one, the next three sections explain the thinking behind it. The sections after that are written for whoever is guiding you, and you can read them too.
How this plan differs

The classic relapse prevention worksheet asks a person to list high-risk situations, warning signs and coping responses, then to avoid the situations. The strongest test of that model, the SOTEP randomised trial, found no reduction in sexual or violent reoffending compared with untreated controls. The men who reoffended less were those who met the goals of treatment, not those who learned a list of triggers.

The program materials in this project reflect this. They replace the traditional relapse prevention plan with an integrated good life, self-regulation and risk-management plan. Approach goals, meaning the life the person is building, are the centre of the plan, and risk factors are treated as obstacles to that life, not as a list of prohibitions. Approach-focused work also improves engagement and honest disclosure of lapses, which helps in a group with mixed motivation and mixed reading ability.
The model in short

The plan is built on the good life the reader wants and the healthy ways of reaching it. Early warning signs and a getting-back-on-track section are kept because they are concrete and useful, but they are parts of the approach-goal structure rather than all of it. The aim is a life that is incompatible with offending, which asks for more than avoiding offending.
Why two separate versions
Online and contact offending do not share the same pathway, so the two plans differ in their risk sections while keeping the same overall skeleton.
Online child exploitation material version
Centres on problematic internet use, the emotional function of viewing, escalation and collecting patterns, and structured, monitored device use.
Gives extra attention to victim awareness, because the absence of a visible victim can feed the belief that no one was harmed.
Avoids a plan built on total internet abstinence, which is unworkable when work, banking and daily life run through the same device.
Contact version
Centres on situations involving access to children, planning ahead, transparency with trusted adults, and supervision conditions.
Treats being alone with a child as a situation to plan around, as part of the wider good-life goals.
Two further components
Living With My Obligations and What I Tell People sit alongside either plan rather than inside it. Both work for a reader working alone, on the same basis as the rest of this component.

Living With My Obligations treats reporting and supervision duties as a planning constraint, not an administrative aside. It states in its own text that it is not legal advice and shows the date it was written. It tells the reader to check the current consolidation of the Community Protection (Offender Reporting) Act 2004 and to raise anything specific to him with the police or a lawyer. Do not add to it or answer questions from it as though you were qualified to give legal advice, whatever your own familiarity with the Act.

What I Tell People prepares a disclosure at three levels, one line, a short version, and a full version, plus what to do if someone already knows or if telling somebody goes badly. The two drafts to watch for are a denial and an over-disclosure that goes into specific detail. The example page in that document takes one of each apart. Your job in the room is the same as the one described there: help him settle on an accurate, brief account that does not grovel, not a script that hides the offence or one that rehearses it.
Running it in the group
The running notes below are for a facilitator and can be skipped if you are working through this yourself. Read the cautions and key resources further down either way.
Build the good life and support sections first. Do not open with the offence or the risk list.
Individualise every plan. The prompts are a scaffold, not a script.
For lower reading levels, read prompts aloud, allow spoken answers to be written down for the person, and use the worked examples as a model.
Treat the plan as a living document. Review and update it as the person changes.
Cautions
The plan is not a risk assessment. Use a validated tool such as the CPORT for online offenders alongside structured professional judgement.
Contact reoffending rates among online-only offenders are low. Do not pitch the plan in a way that overstates contact risk to that group.
No program has yet proven a recidivism reduction specifically for online offenders, so this component is evidence-informed rather than evidence-based.
Integrate supervision and reporting duties under the Community Protection (Offender Reporting) Act 2004 where they apply.
Be clear at the outset about the limits of confidentiality and any mandatory reporting duties.
Key resources
Yates and Prescott, Building a Better Life, and the clinician guide Applying the Good Lives and Self-Regulation Models.
i-SOTP and Inform Plus materials for online-specific content.
Take your time with this short guide to the plan you are going to build.
What the plan is

Your staying-on-track plan does two things at once. One is about the life you want to live, the other about keeping yourself and other people safe. The two belong together, because when your life is going well, staying safe gets easier.
What the plan aims for

You may be expecting a plan full of rules that all start with the word “don’t”. That kind of plan is hard to stick to, and it does not give you much to aim for. Your plan will have a few things to watch out for, but most of it is about what you are building and where you are heading.
Your good life

We start with what you care about. That might be family, friendship, feeling at home, doing good work, learning something, or having some peace of mind. These are ordinary things to want. The plan looks at healthy ways to reach them, so you are not left trying to meet those needs in ways that cause harm.
Spotting when you are drifting

Rough patches come up. The plan helps you notice the early signs that you are slipping off track, such as feeling low, cutting yourself off from people, or using a screen to escape. Noticing early gives you time to act.
If you have a slip
If you have a slip, that is not the same as going all the way back. Your plan lists simple steps to take and people you can call. Reaching out early is a strength, not a failure.
Building it in a group

Build the plan one part at a time. You do not need to be a strong reader. The prompts can be read out loud, and a psychologist or someone you trust can write your answers down for you. Update the plan as things change. If you meet regularly with a psychologist, bring this with you to each session.
Building it on your own

This plan is not tied to a programme, so you might be building it years after one has finished, with nobody looking over your shoulder. Work through it at whatever pace suits you, in whatever order makes sense. Return later to any part you are not ready for. If reading or writing is hard going, use whatever your phone or computer offers for reading text aloud, or talk your answers into a voice recorder and type them up after. It can help to show what you have written to a psychologist or somebody else you trust, but the plan works without anyone.

examples.x: A good answer

examples.label: Good answer to box 3
examples.x: I went through a treatment programme for a sexual offence. I have done a lot of work on it since. I am happy to say more if you want to ask me anything.
examples.why: The answer is about as obvious a version of this box as there is, and it works anyway. It says what happened without minimising it as “trouble” or “a mistake”, and it says that work has been done without asking for sympathy. It stops there, leaving the next word to the other person instead of filling the silence with more explanation. Truthful, brief and finished is what makes a short version work.

examples.x: Common pitfalls

examples.label: Weak answer to box 1
examples.x: Nobody needs to know. It is in the past and it is nobody’s business but mine.
examples.why: This treats the question as whether to tell anyone at all, when the box asks who needs to know because of how they are connected to your life. It closes the box down instead of answering it, and it leaves you unprepared for the person who does ask directly, which is the situation this section is for.

examples.label: Weak answer to box 2
examples.x: I had some legal trouble a while back, it is all sorted now.
examples.why: This phrase is built to close the conversation down fast, and it does not say what happened. If the person already knows anything, being caught minimising it will cost you more trust than an accurate one-liner would have. A one-line version needs to be accurate as well as short.

examples.label: Weak answer to box 4
examples.x: The answer opens well, saying plainly what the offence was and what work has been done since. Then it goes on to describe specific details of what happened and how, the kind of account meant for a psychologist or a court, not for a partner or a close friend.
examples.why: The opening is relevant. The rest goes further than this box asks. A full version is still a summary, and adding detail does not make it more truthful. Somebody else may read this document, so that detail is not safe to write here. If your own answer starts to describe the offending, stop and cross it out.

examples.label: Weak answer to box 6
examples.x: If it goes badly I will just give it some time and it will blow over.
examples.why: The answer is a hope. It does not say what you will do or who you will talk to if a disclosure damages a relationship, so you have no plan at the moment it goes badly.

blocks.x: The little choices that seem to not matter
Every day you make lots of small choices. Most feel like they do not matter much. But small choices join together like links in a chain. One leads to the next.

Some of these choices look harmless on their own. Yet they can slowly lead you towards a risky spot, and away from the life you actually want. Because they seem unimportant, they are easy to miss. That is exactly why they are worth watching.
Here is an example
One of Jay’s good life goals is to be someone his family can trust. Read his chain of choices.
No single choice looks huge. But the chain leads Jay away from being the person he wants to be.
Why this matters
When you see the chain early, you get more chances to change direction. Every link you catch is a chance to steer back towards your good life.

blocks.x: The plan asks a person to work through positions in an offence cycle. The first is a build-up (the situation, the thoughts, and the feelings that preceded an offence). The second is acting out (the thoughts and feelings occurring once the decision to offend had, in practice, already been made). The third is afterward (the feelings that followed and the thoughts used to justify or minimise it). A further position, step-offs, asks for the practical strategies that interrupt the cycle at any of the earlier points.

blocks.head: Differences from the current plan
blocks.x: The Relapse Prevention Plan built for this library uses a different model: an integrated Good Lives and self-regulation plan built around approach goals, not an offence-cycle worksheet (see the Facilitator Brief in Relapse Prevention Plan). That choice rests on the SOTEP randomised trial, which found no reduction in reoffending among men who completed a traditional relapse prevention plan of this kind, compared with untreated controls. This chapter is not a proposal to revert to the earlier model. It keeps the instrument that influenced this programme’s history available to a clinician working with someone who completed it, or comparing the two approaches.
The positions in the cycle
Build-up: situation

The events and circumstances in a person’s life in the lead-up to an offence: relationship strain, financial pressure, isolation, conflict at work, loss, and similar. This position asks what was happening, before it asks what a person felt about it.
Build-up: thoughts
The beliefs and attitudes held about those events before offending, the private case a person was making to himself for why his situation justified what came next.
Build-up: feelings
The emotional state in the period before an offence, both the acute feeling immediately before it and any longer-running mood that had been present for some time.
Acting out: thoughts and feelings

The internal experience during an offence itself: the thoughts that occurred once the decision to offend had effectively already been made, and any shift in feeling from that point of decision through to the end of the act. Consistent with every other worksheet in this library, this position describes internal experience only, never conduct.
Afterward: feelings
The physical and emotional aftermath: relief, shame, confidence, or another feeling entirely, and what, if anything, the behaviour appeared to deliver emotionally in the short term.
Afterward: justifying thoughts
The denial, minimisation or justification used afterward to make the behaviour easier to live with, the account a person gave himself, distinct from any account he may have given anyone else.
Step-offs: strategies

Practical, specific actions intended to interrupt the cycle at whichever position they can be applied to. The original instrument’s own worked example was moving a household computer into a shared family space, a concrete, checkable action rather than a general resolution.
Using this in a session

A facilitator or clinician working with someone who completed this earlier plan can use it as a point of comparison rather than a document to disregard. The useful questions are where the offence-cycle model called attention to something the approach-goal model does not ask about directly, and where the reverse happened. See the Facilitator Brief in Relapse Prevention Plan for the reasoning behind the plan’s current model, and My Plan (online version and contact version), also in Relapse Prevention Plan, for what a person completes now.

If you are the person who completed this earlier plan yourself, this chapter describes your own record, not only a document for somebody else to compare against. You can use it the same way: noticing where the old build-up, acting out, afterward and step-offs questions asked about something your current plan does not, and where your current plan asks about something this one never did.

blocks.head: About this chapter
blocks.x: This chapter is Part B of A Clinician’s Framework: a cannot-act-on-it question, meaning a practice that existed but is not something to do today, not an evidence question, meaning a claim to be checked against research. It describes how SafeCare screened and assessed a person before treatment began, during the programme’s operating years. No facilitator can run it today, and no current version of it exists to opt into or request. It stays here so a clinician working with someone who went through it, or comparing it with current practice, is not working from a gap.

Before intake proper, a caller went through a pre-intake conversation, still anonymous at that stage, that let a person ask questions and hear enough about what the programme involved before committing to it formally.
What intake gathered
At intake, the programme gathered as much history as it reasonably could, for two reasons: it informed treatment, and it gave a benchmark to measure progress against as treatment went on.
The genogram
Drawing a family genogram was a standard part of intake, described in full in Understanding My Past, Concept 7, Your Family Map.
The structured interview

A structured interview covered a person’s history broadly. It asked about drug and alcohol use, mental and physical health, any history of abuse, neglect or violence they had experienced themselves, criminal history, and education and work. It also covered a general psychological profile and a history of the offending itself.
The assessment battery

Alongside the interview, intake included a set of formal tests, psychometric instruments, meaning standardised tests scored the same way for everyone who takes them. Each is named here by what it was and roughly how long it took, not by what a particular answer meant, consistent with how this library treats every such instrument it mentions.
A personality test, around ninety minutes.
A psycho-sexual inventory, around ninety minutes.
An empathy test, around twenty minutes.
A sexual fantasy test, around fifteen minutes.
A questionnaire about attitudes to children and sexuality, around fifteen minutes.

None of these instruments, or their items, are reproduced anywhere in this library. What each measured in general terms (personality, sexual interest patterns, empathy, fantasy content and attitudes) is stated so a clinician knows what intake covered. Nothing here would let anyone administer or score them.
Using this in a session

A facilitator or clinician working with someone who went through this earlier process can use it as background, not a template. It describes what intake used to involve, not what it involves now, and nothing in this chapter authorises reinstating any part of it.

If you are the person who went through this yourself, this chapter is describing your own intake, not only somebody else’s history to be compared against. Reading it back lets you check which parts of it still apply to you and what your current plan and worksheets ask about instead.

blocks.head: About this chapter
blocks.x: This chapter is Part A of A Clinician’s Framework: an evidence question, meaning a claim to be checked against research, not a cannot-act-on-it question, meaning a practice that existed but is not something to do today. It states a theory and explains why it has no evidentiary weight. It does not describe what happened to you or what you are likely to do, and it is not a way of assessing anyone you support. If your own history matches the pattern described below, that alone tells you nothing reliable about yourself or anyone else. Understanding My Past, Concept 9, Patterns: Age, Gender and Form, treats this same ground the same way: as a fact to state, not an explanation to use.
What the theory claims

Gender of Offender Theory holds that a person abused by an offender of the same gender is more likely to go on to offend themselves, while a person abused by an offender of the opposite gender is more likely to experience further victimisation and its long-term effects. The theory is Christabel Chamarette’s own clinical theory, drawn from her observations over SafeCare’s operating years. It has not been peer-reviewed, meaning checked by other researchers before publication, or published. Nor has it been tested against a comparison group, meaning a matched group of people without that abuse history, tracked the same way to see whether the pattern holds up.
Why the reasoning is omitted

The theory’s own reasoning links a person’s later risk to their childhood abuser’s gender in a way that works, in practice, as an explanation for offending rather than an account of it. Concept 9 of Understanding My Past found that this same reasoning does the same thing whichever direction it runs, so reaching for it is usually an excuse, not an accurate account. That finding does not change because the reader of this chapter may be a facilitator rather than the person the pattern describes. A Clinician’s Framework has no separate, more permissive readership, so the reasoning is not set out here either.
The published evidence

One piece of verifiable, published research addresses the general pattern, independent of any theory about gender: Ogloff, Cutajar, Mann and Mullen’s 2012 forty-five year follow-up study, cited in the same chapter of the book. Of male victims of childhood sexual abuse in that study, 5% were later convicted of a sexual offence, rising to 9.2% among those abused at age twelve or older, against 0.6% of a non-abused comparison group. The study is cited here instead of Gender of Offender Theory’s own reasoning, consistent with the rule that the SafeCare book is the authority unless a verifiable published source says otherwise. For anything stated as evidence, this chapter relies on a verifiable published source, not the book’s unpublished theory.
Using this in a session

A facilitator who hears a client use this theory to explain his own abuse history can say what this chapter says: the reasoning has not been shown to predict anything reliably, and using it is usually an excuse rather than an account. The client’s own Concept 9 worksheet, Patterns: Age, Gender and Form, already asks him to state the fact and leave the theory alone. This chapter gives the facilitator the same discipline in professional language, not a different standard.

If you are reading this on your own, you can use the same discipline in the same place: your own Concept 9 worksheet. If your history matches the pattern described above, write it there as a fact and leave it, as that worksheet asks. You do not need anybody in the room to apply it.

blocks.head: About this chapter
blocks.x: This chapter sits outside Part A, Part B and Part C of A Clinician’s Framework. It is not an evidence question about offending, a cannot-act-on-it question about superseded procedure, or a retired instrument. It is the caveat the preamble refers to when it cites Willis and Grace’s finding that better release planning tracked lower sexual recidivism. The preamble gives that finding with a short qualification and sends a treating professional here for the rest. Both consolidated reference documents do the same, in identical wording. This chapter keeps that promise.
What the research shows
What the two studies measured

Willis and Grace built a coding protocol, a fixed scoring guide applied the same way to every file. It scored the quality of release planning for men leaving two New Zealand prison-based treatment programmes for child molesters, Kia Marama in the 2008 study and Te Piriti in the 2009 study. Each was compared against a matched group who did not go on to reoffend. What the protocol scored was never anything the men themselves wrote. It was the reintegration report a treatment coordinator prepared for the Parole Board or Community Probation Service ahead of release. It rated accommodation planning, social support planning, employment planning, and either Good Lives Model secondary goods, meaning the concrete everyday goals a person’s deeper needs get expressed through (2008), or documented idiosyncratic risk factors, meaning warning signs specific to that person rather than a generic list (2009). A separate item recorded the man’s motivation to follow through with the plan, and that item was the treating therapist’s own rating, not anything self-reported.
Correlation and causation

Correlational means two things move together without one being shown to produce the other, as against causal, where one has been shown to bring about the other. Both studies compared existing groups after the fact rather than assigning planning quality at random, so neither can show that better planning caused the better outcome rather than tracking something else that produced both. The 2008 study tested this directly. When IQ and a psychometric measure of dynamic risk, a test score for risk factors that can change over time rather than fixed history, were added as covariates, meaning extra factors statistically held constant to see what was left over, most of the planning items stopped predicting recidivism. Only the accommodation score remained significant. The motivation item is the clearest version of the same problem. A therapist who already saw a man as more settled and more engaged would reasonably write him a fuller plan and rate him as more motivated. In that case the plan and the outcome share a common cause in the man’s presentation, rather than the plan producing the outcome.
Applying it to this workbook

Everything the two studies scored was written by a paid coordinator days before release, about a man who had already been observed by staff for months, for a report that a parole board would go on to read. Every plan in this library is instead written by the reader himself, alone, on his own initiative, at any point after the programme has ended, for nobody’s review. The finding says planning quality once tracked lower reoffending in that professionally supported setting. It does not show, because it was never tested, that a self-directed workbook completed without a coordinator, a parole board or months of observed behaviour reproduces the same pattern.
Using this in a session

A facilitator can tell a client that better planning tracked better outcomes in the published research. The statement is accurate, and he was already told it in the preamble and both reference documents. A facilitator should not present the workbook in front of him as validated by that same evidence, because the instrument that scored those plans was never applied to a document like his. The workbook’s value depends on the reasoning already given in the preamble’s “why bother writing any of this down”, not on statistical weight from a study of somebody else’s paperwork.

If you are the person doing the workbook, the same caution applies to it. The research found that planning quality once tracked a better outcome in a professionally prepared, professionally supervised plan. It has not shown that completing this workbook yourself does the same. That does not reduce the workbook’s value, which depends on the preamble’s reasoning whether or not anybody else ever reads what you write in it.
